Some disappearances are meant to stay buried.And when the assassin’s blade found you, even those faint murmurs ceased. They were gone. Truly, utterly gone.

You penned an edict to the land that once cradled Ansuya, commanding them to swear fealty to their last surviving heir - Princess Ansuya herself - as their new ruler. Truthfully, you had no certainty she would return. Bharat’s influence stretched far; perhaps they had fled beyond reach, vanished into some distant sanctuary. But you wagered that, deep down, they still longed for the soil where they had first met, first loved. You wagered right. The messenger returned with word: Princess Ansuya had stepped forward from the crowd, regal as dawn, and accepted the decree with grace. Then she removed the golden circlet she once wore as consort - and placed it in the messenger’s hands, bidding him deliver it to your new queen. When it reached you, the circlet bore fresh scars of splendor: great, glittering gemstones, each more priceless than the last. And inside the band, etched in delicate script: "Surely these gems cover the rent I owe?"

You entrusted Bharat with all mercantile affairs of the new court - especially the trade routes to foreign lands and tribes.

When the dagger found you, both he and Ansuya were in her domain. Upon hearing the news, Bharat severed every trade route under his control. Prices in the chaotic capital soared; markets stood empty. It hastened the rebel regime's collapse.

But this was all they could do for you. Well... perhaps one thing more. Ansuya built a small shrine in your memory, where she placed fresh white blossoms every dawn.

They never forgot you.

epilogue_2000006.title: Epilogue: Maggie
strings: No matter where you went, Maggie was always by your side. Like a furnace, the hardships you shared fused your hearts into one. You trusted each other completely, and would protect each other no matter what. You raised seven children together, three born to Maggie, and four adopted. They all shared Maggie's wisdom and your character...

No matter where you went, Maggie was always by your side. Like a furnace, the hardships you shared fused your hearts into one. You trusted each other completely, and would protect each other no matter what. Maggie kept a meticulous journal about your travels, all written from her unique and wise perspective. Thousands of years later, though all that you knew would have turned to dust, these travelogues with stories spanning across all the nations of this continent shall remain a vital source for classicists trying to pierce the veil of time. There would be dozens of papers just on the identity of the female author, and you would be remembered as her lovely husband.

The trials of the past have fused all of your hearts together... quite a few too many hearts. As time passed, even suffering and passion faded, and you realized that what kept everyone together might not be your charm, but Maggie's. On suitable days, Maggie would share her other lovers with you, just as they would share you with Maggie. Maggie kept a meticulous journal about this journey of love and romance, all written from her unique and wise perspective. Thousands of years later, though all that you knew would have turned to dust, these travelogues with stories spanning across all the nations of this continent shall remain a vital source for classicists trying to pierce the veil of time. There would be dozens of papers just on the identity of the female author, and you would be remembered as her charming yet infuriating husband.

Maggie took to governance as if born to it - sorting through mountains of neglected edicts, untangling the bureaucratic snarls left in the wake of upheaval. Whispers began trailing in her wake: "Her Highness." An old title, long dormant in court - one reserved for queens in the homeland, though no consort had worn it under the previous Sultan.

As for you, you found the title fitting - and an even more fitting thing to do: you elevated Maggie to be your queen.

She looked radiant in her crown.

Upon confirming your demise, Maggie cast herself from the palace's highest spire - her blood seeping deep into the rose gardens below. Since that day, every soul who dares ascend the golden throne of the Lapis Lazuli Palace, no matter what title they claim... is haunted by visions of a woman turning the pages of a book in the gloom. "Ah, behold yourself," the specter murmurs, her gaze cold with contempt, "Unworthy of my husband's throne. How... pitiful." And it is said: should a ruler dream of her thrice, she will drag them down into the drowning depths of that cursed slumber... never to wake again.

Maggie was taken aback by your decree - though none could deny its logic. She was your wife, your most trusted confidant; and what a fledgling regime needed most was nobility both capable and loyal.

She ordered a smaller chair of silver and ivory placed beside your golden throne, then faced the court veiled in azure gauze embroidered with silver. Her tone was gentle, her counsel sharp, her mind keen - yet when the nobles found no fault in her actions, they turned to slander. "She flaunts her station," they hissed. "A woman has no place stepping from the Sultan's shadow to his side!"

Their words wounded her. So for Maggie's sake - and your own - you bypassed every master and protocol minister, proclaiming her your heir. Should fate strike you down, the empire would be hers. Ah, how the nobles raged! How they shrieked and stamped and groveled! Yet allies emerged - chiefly among the elder noblewomen. They cared little for your rule or how you claimed it, but they never joined the slander. Over pomegranate tea and embroidery, they coolly arranged marriages and courtly whispers...

A grandmother's influence runs deeper than grandfathers dare admit. By season's end, the uproar stilled. Maggie, a woman, was lawfully named heir. And as the Sultan trapped in gilded chains, this act etched your name into eternity.

Maggie nearly staggered when you spoke of the Realm of Game. Clutching her maid's arm, she stared at you, eyes searching, piercing, as if trying to see past your flesh into the soul of the man she once knew... and loved.

After that day, she never spoke to you again. At first, she would linger in your presence, waiting - perhaps hoping - for you to break the silence. But there were far more amusing distractions to occupy a ruler's time than soothing a sulking woman.

In time, you forgot her entirely. Where she dwelled, whom she spoke to, what she ate, whether she lived in health or sickness - none of it mattered. She became just another woman in your harem.

She sat with Sadani, soothing the sudden weeping fits during her pregnancy. She sat with you, her fingers tracing the tension in your back as she whispered of her love. She sat with disgruntled nobles, with dismissed concubines of the fallen court, with every soul in need of steadiness...

The palace could not function without her. You could not fathom how to rule - even for a single minute - without Maggie at your side.

Since that day, every soul who dared ascend the golden throne of the Lapis Lazuli Palace, no matter what title they claimed, was haunted by visions of a woman turning the pages of a book in the gloom.

And it was said: should a ruler dream of her thrice, she would drag them down into the drowning depths of that cursed slumber... never to wake again.

Maggie was your queen then, the mother of the realm.

The royal gown of the new realm had been a single length of heavy silk, embroidered from hem to collar. To dress her, two maids would hold the fabric aloft while a third knelt to shift its train, and a fourth fastened the gem-studded golden sash about her waist with rubies and diamonds glittering like frozen blood and winter stars.

Sometimes, you dismissed the maids and dressed her yourself. The two of you laughed as the silk slipped through your fingers, as jewels clattered to the floor, as the sash tumbled undone again and again, until your mirth shook the very hangings of the bedchamber.

She had been the most beautiful queen.

In these moments of joy, you felt yourself becoming [player.name] once more - not the king, nor the sultan, nor the Starrenegade with Crimson Robe - just being yourself.

As your queen, Maggie received the news of your death with solemn grace.

From that day forth, she withdrew to the deepest prayer chamber in the palace. No longer did she wear the royal silks, only simple black robes. Her hair hung loose, unadorned by jewel or braid.

Day and night she prayed. That’s not for your soul's peace, for she knew full well you would be honored among the dead. Only one plea passed her lips:

That death might come for her at the proper hour. Not too soon, for the Sultan's loyal nobles still watched her every move, and she would not have her passing disturb the realm you built. Nor too late, for she longed to join you in the world beyond.

From the moment you forged this realm, Maggie counseled you, warned you, until you grew weary of this vexing woman and turned away.

She took her own life after you death.

For many years, King Sirshana's court stood without a queen, for he felt himself already bound by the throne and would suffer no woman's chains.

Thus it fell to Maggie to perform a queen's duties, attending court at your side, receiving courtiers' wives, turning away would-be concubines, and selecting suitable ladies-in-waiting.

Under her guidance, the realm abolished the eunuch system. Serving girls were taught to read, no longer mere chattel to be married off at coming of age. Those who proved capable might remain in service, taking on greater responsibilities alongside Maggie.

Sirshana would sometimes jest, "If ever I take a wife, let her be like yours." Years later, Maggie indeed found him a clever girl of tribal royalty whose skin the color of honey, eyes like molten caramel, smile that shone like stars, and heart as bright as Maggie's own.

Their wedding was a splendid affair. You stood as witness, Maggie as matchmaker. Following your homeland's tradition, you both escorted the bridal couple before hundreds of thousands, where a procession that stirred memories of your own wedding day...

You turned to glance at Maggie, and found her already looking at you.

She was as beautiful as she'd been on that day.

For years, King Sirshana's palace stood without a mistress, and so Maggie often accompanied you to court, tending to duties that should have fallen to a queen.

She hosted flawless feasts, dismissed all eunuchs with a decree that no more such wretched souls should be made, taught the serving women their letters, and conversed with foreign envoys' wives - perfection woven through every thread of court life.

On nights when weariness weighed upon you both, she would lean against your shoulder and muse about what sort of maiden might please Sirshana. One with honeyed skin and caramel eyes, perhaps? A clever, kind girl with a smile like sunlight... Yet these talks always ended in silence. The Sirshana of today seemed beyond happiness. He was as weary, as torn, and as broken as yourself.

But you still had Maggie, at least.

When word came of Sirshana's fall, Maggie first trembled, then grew pensive.

"I always thought he was waiting for this day..." she said to you, "Remember? He'd say he was no true king... When I sought to match him with that tribal princess, said what a beauty she was, like a pearl of honeyed gold! But he answered, 'I'll not wear the crown long, but she deserves to be queen all her days.' Aye... those were his words. Now I understand."

You let out a heavy sigh together.

Where the last Sultan's harem had had no mistress, only slave girls, yet your palace held a queen - Maggie.

Her gowns were no richer than other noblewomen's, save for the slender ruby-studded circlet upon her brow. Yet she toiled more than them all: settling affairs of state at your side, disbanding the harem, hosting foreign envoys, ending the making of eunuchs...

When the long day ended, she would curl against you, sharing the hookah's smoke while murmuring of the day's deeds. Then the weariness took her. She would drift asleep in your arms, light as a feather yet heavy as an anchor holding a ship safe in harbor.

By her side, you always slept soundly.

With the help of her handmaid, Maggie fled. She wrapped her face in tattered scarves and smeared dung over her skin to mask the scent of perfume - tricks enough to fool the mob's crude senses.

She found your corpse first, and gave it proper rites. Only then did she take the dagger to her own heart.

Maggie too was saved, hidden in a water barrel smuggled from the palace. The cart-driver and watermen were eunuchs whose freedom you had granted, the men who kept faith with you and the queen.

You reunited with her on a sunlit hill where your loyalists had built a fine wooden cottage. Its window framed the distant capital like a painted miniature.

Broken as you were, her care mended you swiftly. Your supporters came seldom as the realm was still in chaos. Yet you wanted for nothing. Fresh vegetables appeared at dawn. Silent fishermen left buckets of gleaming catch. Shoes and fabrics on the doorstep after dark.

And books. Maggie would often find them in the garden, wrapped in oilcloth like buried treasure. She gathered them as one plucks ripe pomegranates. At night, she would light a lamp and press against you as you read together, letting the cool evenings slip away between pages.

Was life always this simple and sweet? Or did nearly dying make every ordinary thing glow like gilded sunlight?

The answer mattered not.

Through sorrow and despair, through joy and laughter, Maggie stood by your side.

She bore half your burdens of rule. At her command, the old Sultan's harem was dissolved where those women fairly compensated, servants freed from bondage to earn wages. She ended the making of eunuchs, forbade the use of children for menial labor. Under her order, a whole wing of the palace became a scriptorium for scribes to record the new regime's decrees, and many of those scribes were women who'd followed Maggie willingly.

Your opponents might sneer that you leaned on your wife's counsel. You took it as praise: if it vexed them so, let them find wives worth leaning on.

You grumbled sometimes, for how Maggie's duties left her no time to curl against you. She sighed in turn, for how you heeded every courtier's words by day, yet fell asleep too weary to hear hers by night.

Grievances were traded, then swiftly pardoned. Stolen moments became embraces.

A Sultan with a true companion, that alone was a wonder beyond wonders.

Maggie scoured the chaos of the palace with desperate fury, until at last she found your broken form pinned beneath the Golden Throne.

She insisted they pry the throne apart and drag you free. She dressed you anew, chose the fairest spot in the palace's old rose garden where the blooms were richest, and laid you to rest with her own hands.

When it was done, she took up your blade and slit her own throat.

Maggie had never been so angry, never!

While you lay unconscious, she gnashed her teeth and dragged forth the high noble who had stirred the mob to storm the palace. She overruled all objections and had his head lopped off. Those who had carried the battering ram to break down the palace gates were gelded and made eunuchs, while hundreds more who had joined the looting faced her ruthless justice.

By the time you awoke, the entire court trembled beneath Maggie's wrath. Maggie, the Sultan's wife and the Vizier, had shown them all that cruelty was not difficult. The only reason you had never wielded it was because you wished to be a great Sultan.

After that, even when you had recovered enough to walk unaided, Maggie refused to let you move through the palace alone. She would take your arm, steady you, muttering for you to rest.

The court still feared her, yet she took some pleasure in that. These days, the nobles obeyed her far more swiftly than before.

After consulting with you, Maggie entrusted Riel to proclaim the decree abolishing the eunuch system. For centuries, this land had perpetuated the cruel practice of creating wretched, mutilated men. But now, it was finally ended.

"That eased my heart," Maggie told you. "To set right something so twisted... it is deeply satisfying."

You ran your fingers through her smooth, long hair, silently agreeing.

When your corpse was brought back to the palace, Maggie stood waiting on the steps with pale. She spoke of a dream from the night before: a golden fish, beautiful and winged, soaring toward the heavens... only to be struck down by a stone.

She threw herself upon your body and wept, her cries echoing through the silent courtyard. The gathered crowd dared not speak, nor dared they pull her away.

When at last someone summoned the courage to touch her shoulder, they found her chest drenched in blood. She had taken your blade to her throat, and joined you in death.

Maggie wandered with you through exile and hardship, never once uttering a complaint. Instead, after each trial, in each new place, she would conjure some small comfort: a picnic by a lakeshore, the sweet smoke of local hookah, a haunting ballad or a ribald epic.

And in time, a quiet truth took root in your heart: this was no exile, not truly. Wherever Maggie stood, that was home. And you had never left it.

Under Maggie's command, your court abolished the eunuch system entirely. The empire's ancient tradition of mutilating men to guard harems had ended with your reign.

She then disbanded the bloated harems left by the previous Sultan, where over seven hundred women languished, including inherited from past rulers, though fewer than two hundred had ever known a Sultan's touch.

Once emptied, the sprawling chambers were repurposed: scribes took up residence, the royal library expanded, and a new garden bloomed beside the old rose garden.

Now, between the burdens of rule, you often slip away to Maggie's garden. She greets you with a cup of honeyed pomegranate tea, a pipe of perfectly blended smoke, and the most intriguing book at hand.

With her there, the palace is no longer a gilded cage. It is home.

From the first, Maggie had opposed your decision to go to the fire. She spoke of a dream: olden fish, beautiful and winged, soaring toward the heavens... only for the sky to turn to flame and swallow it whole.

After the dagger found your heart, she steeled herself. With Alim and courtiers, she hunted the assassins and steadied the realm. Only a year later did she don the black veil and bear your bones back to the land where you had wed.

There she remained, teaching girls their letters and embroidery, tending the garden where you slept. She never took another to her heart.

Maggie was shaken to the bone by your near-brush with death. She turned ruthless in vetting all who sought entry to the palace, and insisted you never stir beyond its walls without a full complement of Iron Guards, and without her by your side.

You raised no objection. Now, the two of you have become virtually inseparable.

With Nawfal's harem standing empty, utterly devoid of souls. Maggie assumed some duties of the palace's mistress.

She received foreign envoys, hosted lavish feasts, changed the court's adornments with the seasons, and granted every eunuch and slave-girl their freedom, forbidding forever the making of more such pitiful, broken souls.

Nawfal treated her with respect. On occasion, he would invite Nawfal to take tea in the old rose garden, where they spoke of statecraft, of books lately read, of poetry newly in fashion.

And while they enjoyed such pleasures, you were in the council chambers, locked in battle with scheming nobles. Even if Maggie always returned with gifts and sweetmeats for you, even if all the court whispered that the Sultan was trying to honor the Speaker of Council by respecting his wife.

But, you still felt... Ah! It really rankled.

Maggie too was saved, hidden in a water barrel smuggled from the palace. The cart-driver and watermen were eunuchs whose freedom you had granted, the men who kept faith with you and your wife.

You reunited with her on a sunlit hill where your loyalists had built a fine wooden cottage. Its window framed the distant capital like a painted miniature.

Broken as you were, her care mended you swiftly. Your supporters came seldom as the realm was still in chaos. Yet you wanted for nothing. Fresh vegetables appeared at dawn. Silent fishermen left buckets of gleaming catch. Shoes and fabrics on the doorstep after dark.

And books. Maggie would often find them in the garden, wrapped in oilcloth like buried treasure. She gathered them as one plucks ripe pomegranates. At night, she would light a lamp and press against you as you read together, letting the cool evenings slip away between pages.

Was life always this simple and sweet? Or did nearly dying make every ordinary thing glow like gilded sunlight?

The answer mattered not.

Through sorrow and despair, through joy and laughter, Maggie stood by your side.

With Nawfal's harem empty, she took upon herself the duties of a palace mistress. At her command, the old Sultan's harem was dissolved where those women fairly compensated, servants freed from bondage to earn wages. She ended the making of eunuchs, forbade the use of children for menial labor. Under her order, a whole wing of the palace became a scriptorium for scribes to record the new regime's decrees, and many of those scribes were women who'd followed Maggie willingly.

Your opponents might sneer that you leaned on your wife's counsel. You took it as praise: if it vexed them so, let them find wives worth leaning on.

On your throne is a dragon-slaying relief, based on Maggie's original sketch. Her embroidery expertise portrayed your conquering act with exceptional accuracy, far more striking than reality.

She applied this design to a deep blue veil — chosen for its optimal gold thread contrast — and as the mistress of the Dragonslaying Sultan's harem, Maggie wore it, inspiring envy in noblewomen throughout the land. Subsequent popularity thrust the dragon-slaying motif into empire-wide embroidery trends, with your visage replicated across numerous hands, at times confronting dragons no larger than puppies, and sometimes warriors with dragon wings.

Even post-mortem, this image flourishes through generations, every artisan imprinting their take on you and the dragon, immortalizing your legacy across time.

Maggie marched with you through every campaign, mending your armor, binding your wounds, and penning those painfully courteous replies to Nawfal on your behalf.

Just as when you were caught in the Sultan's game, she never once complained. Though sometimes, if you listened closely, you might catch the faintest sigh.

Somehow, without you noticing, Maggie had ceased speaking to you altogether. She took to avoiding you, losing herself for hours in the palace gardens.

Perhaps it was for the best. You could not bear to see disappointment in her eyes.

epilogue_2000008.title: Epilogue: Ansuya
strings:
Ansuya lowered her eyes and made her request with practiced meekness: she wished to go home.

"My father and brothers gifted me to the Sultan like some bauble, hoping to buy his mercy. They were slaughtered for their stupidity - a fitting end." Her lips curled in a thin, joyless smile. "But my homeland... it was beautiful. I would retire there, if my master permits."

What reason had you to refuse? She departed before the next moonrise.

You secured Ansuya a place at court, granting her mastership over her ancestral lands. With those who had bartered her to the Sultan's pleasures now lying in unmarked graves, she stood - by cruel irony - as the last legitimate scion of that blighted bloodline. When the decree was proclaimed, messengers and envoys from her homeland swarmed about her like carrion birds to fresh meat. She laughed. Then wept. Then laughed again - a broken marionette of emotions, her tongue rendered useless by the weight of it all.

epilogue_2000009.title: Epilogue: Sadani
strings:
You granted Sadani noble standing, permitting her continued presence at court - partly to appease the old guard (for she was once a consort!), and partly because Sadani was iron-willed, her cutting sneers and withering disdain proving useful tools.

Upon her appointment, she vanished for a time, long enough to birth a child, some whispered - before striding back into court with renewed arrogance. Indeed, she became an invaluable ally, reading your will in the slightest glance and delivering the necessary verdicts in matters too delicate for your direct hand.

Years passed. Then, without warning, Sadani adopted a child. The court buzzed with outrage - "She grows restless in her widowhood!" they hissed. "That is no foundling, but her own bastard!" Worse still, they muttered of the veiled guard she kept in her household, a shadowed figure whose presence reeked of impropriety...

"Let those who take issue challenge him to a duel," Sadani remarked idly, examining her nails. "He has sworn to defend my honor unto death. And do recall - this matter was already brought before the Sultan."

Ah. So the Sultan knew... well then.

The matter was dropped.

Seliman returned to court, his face bare once more.

Of the erstwhile Sadani, no whisper reached your ears, but you attended Seliman's wedding. His radiant bride cradled a boy whose features mirrored his own with uncanny precision, proudly and blissfully.

The assembled nobles gaped like fish hauled onto dry land. This woman called "Sadani" bore the late consort's face, yet when you raised your goblet in toast, the message rang clearer than temple bells: The new Sultan sanctioned this farce. Ah. So the Sultan knew... well then.

The matter was dropped.

Seliman returned to court, his face bare once more. As for Sadani - once a consort - vanished for precisely the length of time required to birth a child, then strode back into court with all the imperious bearing of a woman who had turned scandal into power. Bound by law from remarrying, she wore her disgrace like a coronet.

Years later came the child - a boy with Seliman's sharp features and, some whispered, his temper. When tongues began wagging, Sadani - now styled as Master Sadani - bared her fangs: "Shall a woman be denied the comfort of a child's laughter? Must orphaned beauty now be suspect?"

Her words cut deeper than any blade, her fury a weapon honed in palace intrigues. The murmurs died quickly enough when Seliman - that hulking relic of royal favor - offered "honorable satisfaction" to the most vocal critics. Strange how few cared to cross swords with a Iron Guard who had survived two sultans' reigns. The matter was dropped.

The former Iron Guard and the consort knelt before you - Seliman and Sadani, pleading for your leave to disappear from your sight forever. You granted it. They say aboard the ship that carried them from the land of the New Sun, Sadani gave birth to a comely boy. To all who asked, she claimed she was but a merchant's daughter, her husband a simple blacksmith - that neither had ever laid eyes upon any Sultan, past or present.

You bestowed a noble status on Sadani, allowing her to continue frequenting your court. This was partly to pacify the traditional elite — after all, she had been a consort! — and partly because Sadani was a formidable woman; her sneers and disdain were quite useful.

She was indeed a loyal supporter of yours, willing to articulate the conclusions you desired in politically thorny situations according to your cues.

The matter was dropped.

Sadani fled the harem within hours of your overthrow of the last Sultan. She was a clever woman, and knew what you intended.

The former Iron Guard, Seliman vanished at the same hour.

Seliman visited the Queen Mother and the young Sultan often. At first, he took care to avoid your gaze, then ceased to bother. His face would flush with joy at the sight of the boy, and when the little Sultan played with the wooden sword and shield he'd carved, the man looked near tears.

The court buzzed with whispers about them, yet you saw no need to punish the gossips overmuch. The realm was firmly in your grip, and the question of the boy's bloodline... well, that might prove a useful weapon in time.

And of course, whenever Sadani begged you to remind Seliman to beware of his discourtesy and others’ whispers, you obliged. But if the man could not hide his happiness, that was hardly your fault.

Seliman remained a Iron Guard, standing proud whenever Her Grace, the Queen Mother entered court with the young Sultan in her arms. His face betrayed a joy he could never conceal. When the boy fell ill, even a mere sniffle ora cough, the man would fret like a Headless chick, near ready to drag the court physicianr to the royal chambers by his chain.

And of course, whenever Sadani begged you to remind Seliman to beware of his discourtesy and others' whispers, you obliged. But if the man could not hide his happiness, that was hardly your fault.

After your death, Sadani took up the regency. Each morning she would sit upon the golden throne with the young Sultan cradled in her arms.

She had orchestrated the assassination well enough, but ruling proved another matter. Fear had driven her to this. Fear for her life, for her child. And so she drove Seliman, who in turn drove the fate of the realm.

No matter how she tried to mask her inexperience, the nobles smelled blood. The old nobles, long suppressed under your rule, flocked to her side, hailing her as the saint who had purged a usurper, then demanding privileges greater than any Sultan before had granted. Your reformers sneered and refused to bend the knee, calling her a regicide who had strangled the realm's last hope for peace. And why else would Seliman do such a thing, they whispered, unless the boy was his own?

Sadani broke beneath the onslaught. She wept before the court, clutching her son. Her tears had once softened a Sultan's heart, had once moved a Iron Guard's soul... but now they meant nothing. They only invited cruelty.

Her son was dead before his fourth nameday, poisoned. And she followed soon after. Then came the claimants, seven at least, sprouting like weeds from every corner of the realm. And so the long, bloody chaos began.

Seliman was spared the sight of his son's death. After driving his blade through your heart, he cried, "Glory to the Sultan!", then opened his own throat. He feared his life would cast doubt upon the boy's bloodline. Worse, he feared living long enough to see suspicion darken Sadani's eyes, for what father does not hunger for his son's power?

So he served his woman one last time, and died content.

Sadani bore a son, the next Sultan, under your watchful eye. You had the child taken from her at once, given to wet nurses, permitting her but one visit every seven days.

She wept, of course. You told her it was for the boy’s safety, for who knew what vipers lurked in the harem, eager to strike at her and her babe? To be certain, you slit the throats of every maid who had attended her, leaving only mute eunuchs to guard her.

She tried to take her own life, more than once. The eunuchs stopped her each time. When she refused to eat, you brought the child before her and pinched his tender flesh until he wailed. Sadani yielded at last, broken. She should have done so sooner.

Your realm remained peaceful and happy.

After you took Sadani into your "protective custody," Seliman made several attempts to steal her away from the harem.

So long as he kept struggling, Sadani clung to foolish hope which makes defiance linger.

Amusing as their little drama was... you had to order Seliman's head struck off and tossed at Sadani's feet.

She became far more obedient afterward.

The traitors put Sadani on display, forcing her to hold the infant Sultan upon her lap each morning court was held. The little ruler sat stiffly upon his mother's knees, tugging at her braids and babbling cheerfully. Sadani, however, was not cheerful for that. Her chains were tighter now than under your rule. The realm had fractured with your fall. Wars flared in every province. The traitors feared she might yet reach out to your loyalists, that she might turn the tide back in your name. And if that happened, their deaths would be neither quick nor kind.

So they formed a council to rule in the Sultan's stead. Every eunuch and handmaid who had served Sadani was put to the sword, replaced with strangers. The child's wet nurses were slain one after another. For days, the royal babe went hungry, yet his mother's milk dried up by grief. Your loyalists struck back from every corner of the realm. Now it was the traitors who trembled, who lay awake at night.

And so, in a room ringed with guards, under a thousand watching eyes... somehow Sadani found a blade. She gently covered her son's eyes. Then, when the maids looked away, opened her own throat.

She left no final words. The traitors hastily declared her mad. They scrambled for new wet nurses; the child suckled at a different breast each day. The motherless boy did not live to see his second nameday. With his death, the line of Sultans ended.

The war you left behind raged on. The realm split asunder. And in the halls of the dead... perhaps you and Sadani sit in silence, facing one another at last.

Sadani soon gave birth to a healthy son who was declared by the noble council as Shilhak-Inshushinak-Shutruk-Nahhunte III. She had wished to name him Shulana, after the Star-Souled of longevity, but you counseled patience. "Do not provoke them at the naming," you warned.

Such cautious whispers had always passed between you and Sadani. Sometimes she stayed your hand when prideful nobles tested you. Sometimes you stopped her from punishing the haughty wives of courtiers. Together, you guarded the throne and little Shilhak III (though his mother still called him Shulana in private). One day, when he came of age and took the reins of power, you might both breathe easier.

Yet distrust lingered between you. She wondered if you would truly surrender authority to her son. You wondered if the boy, grown to manhood, would show gratitude... or a blade. The crown you shared was already thin, yet now split in two.

But for today, tomorrow, the day after - for as long as you could endure - Sadani still trusted you. When her precious child cried "Uncle [player.name]!" and rushed into your arms, the smile in her eyes remained true.

Seliman visited the Queen Mother and the young Sultan often. At first, he took care to avoid your gaze, then ceased to bother. His face would flush with joy at the sight of the boy, and when the little Sultan played with the wooden sword and shield he'd carved, the man looked near tears.

The court buzzed with whispers about them, you had to remind Sadani to be cautious. She scolded Seliman publicly, demanding proper deference, but the man refused restraint.

When the Sultan turned five, Sadani ordered Seliman's death. They say he showed no fear, only remorse, yet apologizing for the trouble he had brought upon her and the child.

Seliman remained a Iron Guard, standing proud whenever Her Grace, the Queen Mother entered court with the young Sultan in her arms. His face betrayed a joy he could never conceal. When the boy fell ill, even a mere sniffle ora cough, the man would fret like a Headless chick, near ready to drag the court physicianr to the royal chambers by his chain.

The court buzzed with whispers about them. Each time the rumor surfaced, the man would publicly challenge the slanderer, for such vile lies dishonored both Queen Mother and the Sultan. And you, the Regent, would solemnly declare that such duels only strengthened the realm, for what better lesson to the little Sultan than witnessing true valor?

After a few blades were bloodied, the whispers died, at least within the walls, at least before your eyes.

As for the common folks... well, let them talk. Watch how Seliman's face lighted up when the boy reached for him, did the man not deserve some measure of joy?

A few months before the dagger found you, you sought out Sadani and Seliman and spoke plain: they must flee the realm, and swiftly. Sadani's belly would soon betray her. She could not name the father openly, that would mark her a faithless whore, fit only for stoning. Nor could she claim the child was the Sultan's, lest she share power with Zazie and earn a noose for her troubles. Flight was their only path. You had secured a ship bound for foreign shores and tight-lipped sailors. They should leave that very night.

The pair fell to their knees, weeping thanks, and were gone.

They say aboard the ship that carried them from the empire, Sadani gave birth to a comely boy. To all who asked, she claimed she was but a merchant's daughter, her husband a simple blacksmith - that neither had ever laid eyes upon any Sultan, past or present.

You granted Sadani noble status, allowing her continued presence in your court; Zazie enthusiastically approved, remarking that she never disliked Sadani, especially admiring how she pretended no knowledge of her involvement with the Iron Guard.

After her appointment, Sadani disappeared entirely—long enough to have a child—before haughtily returning to court, alleging only a bout with fever... to which you and Zazie shared a laugh.

Years later, Sadani suddenly adopted a child, sparking disapproval from some, accusing her of restlessly discontent, owning the child herself; moreover, a concealed servant was harbored at her residence, raising eyebrows...

"Oh, dissatisfied individuals may duel this servant; he claims undying efforts to protect my honor," Sadani casually declared,
 
"Do remember, this matter has already been reported to the Queen Dowager and the Regent."

The matter was dropped.

Seliman returned to court, his face bare once more.

Of the erstwhile Sadani, no whisper reached your ears, but you attended Seliman's wedding. His radiant bride cradled a boy whose features mirrored his own with uncanny precision, proudly and blissfully.

The assembled nobles gaped like fish hauled onto dry land. This woman called "Sadani" bore the late consort's face, yet when you and Zazie raised your goblets in toast, the message rang clearer than temple bells: just keep silence. The matter was dropped.

The former Iron Guard and the consort knelt before you - Seliman and Sadani, pleading for your leave to disappear from your sight forever. You granted it. When Zazie heard, she laughed until tears wet her cheeks. "She could never outplay me... That man suits her as well as the Golden Throne suits me! Oh, my poor, cast-off Sadani. Just let her go. You did right."

They say aboard the ship that carried Seliman and Sadani from the empire, Sadani gave birth to a comely boy. To all who asked, she claimed she was but a merchant's daughter, her husband a simple blacksmith - that neither had ever laid eyes upon any Sultan, past or present.

epilogue_2000010.title: Epilogue: Zazie
strings: Zazie came to you on the night of your coronation - her figure alluring, her skin dusted with gold, the intoxicating scent of foreign perfumes clinging to her as she moved. She leaned close, her voice a velvet whisper, promising how well she could serve you... Your head spun, and for a fleeting moment, you understood why the late Sultan had lavished so much time and gold upon her. Then Maggie arrived with her retinue. She strode past Zazie without so much as a glance, and her scribe cleared his throat, reciting the ancient imperial decree: No woman who has shared a Sultan's bed may wed another. Zazie only laughed, clapping Maggie on the shoulder - not in anger, but in approval. "Well done," she said, amused. You wasted no time sending her away, and she departed without protest, her belongings filling an entire ship. "I shall find another Sultan worthy of my service," were her last words.

She leaned close, her voice a velvet whisper, promising how well she could serve you... Your head spun, and for a fleeting moment, you understood why the late Sultan had lavished so much time and gold upon her. You took her into your harem, though the court whispered it was forbidden for a woman to warm two Sultans' beds. But Zazie was intoxicating, and you were determined to pluck this golden flower. She became the jewel of your court - until, some seven or eight years later, she and her son would climb over your slowly poisoned corpse to claim the throne. But that is another tale. For now... enjoy the feast before you.

Zazie departed the harem soon after, her belongings laden upon an entire ship. The laws of the empire forbade a Sultan's concubine from taking another husband - so she would seek a land ignorant of such decrees, a realm untouched by the New Sun's reach. There, she would weave her charms anew, until some other ruler knelt to adorn her in gold and jewels. You never heard word of her again.

You raised Zazie to nobility, granting her the right to remain in the capital and walk the halls of the palace at will. She found your decision... perplexing. In her world, a Sultan either desired a woman or wished her dead - this notion of pure benevolence made no sense to her. "Ah, so you elevate me to spite other women? Clever. Truly, you were born to rule." Before you could correct her, she had already thrown herself into Buthayna's brothel trade with glee. Indeed, the empire's ancient laws forbade a Sultan's women from remarrying - but they said nothing about her owning a brothel. A loophole, as far as she was concerned.

Zazie showed utmost deference at your coronation. She blessed you, knelt before you, and begged leave to scrape out her days in the realm, swearing never to breathe a word of what passed between you.

After the dagger found you, she strode into the palace with her son in her arms. The rebels proclaimed the boy the rightful heir of the late Sultan, and so Zazie became Regent.

For all its legitimacy, this new reign lacked much else. The child took a chill at two and a half, then perished between dusk and dawn. Zazie wept, refusing all hands near the little Sultan's corpse. "I'll find another boy to crown!" she shrieked.

Madness had taken her. So they put her to the sword.

After your coronation, Zazie fled. She took with her a hundred chests of treasure. No one knew when she'd amassed such wealth, or how she'd spirited it all away unseen.

In the years that followed, she became favored concubine to at least two kings and three city lords. Later still, she came to a remote island with a brood of highborn children, crowned herself queen, and spent the rest of her days drowning untamed ambitions and desires.

When you first ascended the throne, Zazie proposed leaving the country and taking her accustomed eunuchs, maids, and, of course, her property. "These were gifts from the one you overthrew; surely you wouldn't deprive a woman of her property, right?"

Overwhelmed with work, you absentmindedly agreed.

Thus, Zazie embarked with over forty people and more than 160 chests of treasures. She perfectly evaded all political turmoil following your assassination. When the capital resounded with wails, she had already landed on a distant western island, charming its chieftain completely.

Over two years, she gradually increased the dose of poison, eventually killing the chieftain. Zazie and her newborn child became the rulers of the island; she acquired the promised power.

For days after your coronation, Zazie tried every art to seduce you. Golden bells hung from her full breasts, chiming as she made them dance; praises to your glory were written along her inner thighs, the endings hidden where only a determined gaze might reach. Then you announced your plans for the Realm of Game.

The golden concubine vanished, replaced by a woman in heavy traveling garb, kneeling before you with her retinue. "Let me take my handmaids and go," she begged. "A woman who warmed the last Sultan’s bed is unfit for the next."

You granted her leave. Then made certain the court knew exactly how much gold slithered away in her chests. When word came that Zazie had chartered a great ship, you took special care to distribute extra Bloodshed Tickets among the dockworkers.

She was clever enough to see you were worse than the last Sultan. She was clever enough to run. But you’ve always loved a cat-and-mouse game best.

You raised Zazie to nobility, granting her the right to linger in the capital and walk the palace halls at will.

She understood at once. She was to be your Golden mark, a target for every vice: Carnality, Extravagance, Conquest, Bloodshed. Pale with fury, she demanded what price might buy back her life.

By the time she fled the palace alive and unharmed, vanishing to gods know where, every last grain of gold she'd scraped from the late Sultan's corpse had found its way back into your pocket.

Zazie loathed you.

She carried a child who could have been Sultan, why had you chosen that Sadani over her?

Worse still, as Regent, you had stripped away everything the late Sultan had gifted her: the golden bathing pool, the jeweled curtains, the jade tub that flowed with etheric essence. She could have remained in the harem, yes, but there would be no lovers, no flatterers, no path to power. What use had living like that been? Frantically, she had sought out your enemies, whispering that her unborn babe should rule. But years spent pleasuring a late ruler had left her no allies among the nobles.

On the night Sadani went into labor, while the palace burned with activity, Zazie fled. She took every treasure she could carry: pouches of gold coins, slippers wrought with delicate filigree, the golden threads braided into her hair. Only the child she left behind. What good had a dead Sultan's son been to his mother?

To your surprise, Maggie took the babe in with open arms. Even Sadani admitted it, there had been no calculation in Maggie's kindness. She had doted on the boy with such pure delight that none dared tear him from her.

And so, your halls grew livelier still.

Zazie loathed you.

She carried a child who could have been Sultan, why had you chosen that Sadani over her?

Worse still, as Regent, you had stripped away everything the late Sultan had gifted her: the golden bathing pool, the jeweled curtains, the jade tub that flowed with etheric essence. She could have remained in the harem, yes, but there would be no lovers, no flatterers, no path to power. What use had living like that been? Frantically, she had sought out your enemies, whispering that her unborn babe should rule. But years spent pleasuring a late ruler had left her no allies among the nobles.

On the night Sadani went into labor, while the palace burned with activity, Zazie fled. She took every treasure she could carry: pouches of gold coins, slippers wrought with delicate filigree, the golden threads braided into her hair.

You never saw her again. The fate of the child she carried remained a mystery lost to the winds.

Zazie watched with cold eyes as you placed Sadani upon the throne.

On the night of coronation, she leaned close and whispered in your ear:

"You are a coward, too afraid to claim the throne for yourself. Were it me, I would have taken it."

Without waiting for reply, she turned and vanished into the revelry.

Only at dawn did you discover her flight, and the missing chests of gold and jewels she'd taken with her into the night.

You commanded Zazie to remain at court as your official, to serve the empire. She said nothing, only nodded.

And serve she did, untangling the messy affairs of the previous reign, overseeing the dismissal of the late Sultan's concubines... all while her belly swelled day by day. Whispers slithered through the halls: This child, too, carries the Sultan's blood. Whoever births a son first - Zazie or Sadani - shall be the true mother of the next ruler, right?

On the eve of Zazie's labor, she came to you under cover of night.

"Still you hesitate, Regent?" Her gaze was sharp as a blade. "Every day I feel this child kick within me... a strong boy. He could be Sultan."

You told her Sadani's child would wear the crown, but hers would live free as a nobleman, unburdened by power. The kinder fate, surely. Though, if she wished, you could grant Sadani death instead. But you had no taste for spilling a child's blood, but neither would you flinch from necessity.

"Ah," she said, arching a brow. "The Regent keeps a spare heir, a leash for that fool Sadani. Clever."

You did not deny it. After that night, you spoke no more, until the day she vanished, abandoning her swaddled babe to flee the palace forever.

The child thrived in Maggies care. He was free, happy, and far from the weight of crowns.

Zazie loathed you. By what right did you choose that Sadani over her?

But as she came to understand your Realm of game, that hatred curdled into fear. She knew her own worth in Golden Bloodshed and Carnality, and she had seen how masterfully you played the game.

So when you became Regent, Zazie tried to flee the realm. Worse, she dared take the late Sultan's treasures with her. You caught her, of course.

To take her would be Golden Carnality; to kill her would be Golden Bloodshed. But to scatter her stolen gold among the trembling onlookers? That was Golden Extravagance. The lesson burned so deep that no soul dared cross you for years to come.

And that was the best Conquest. You were the gamer, weren’t you?

When you first became regent, Zazie suggested leaving the country with her accustomed eunuchs, maids, and, of course, her property. "These were given by the one you overthrew; surely you wouldn't strip a woman of her property, right?"

Busy beyond measure, you agreed without much thought.

Hence, Zazie and over forty individuals set sail with over 160 chests of treasures. She skillfully avoided all political upheaval after your assassination. While the capital was filled with lamentations, she charmed a chieftain on a far-off isle.

Over two years, she slowly increased the poison dosage, assassinating the chieftain. With her newborn, she became the island's sovereign, attaining the power she was promised.

You raised Zazie to nobility, granting her the right to remain in the capital and walk the halls of the palace at will.

She found your decision... perplexing. In her world, a Sultan either desired a woman or wished her dead - this notion of pure benevolence made no sense to her.

"Ah, so you elevate me to spite other women? Clever. Truly, you were more Sultan than the last one," she said, "Why don't you take the throne? Or is playing Regent more amusing? You'd rather pull strings than wear crowns... how delightfully wicked of you!"

Before you could correct her, she had already thrown herself into Buthayna’s brothel trade with glee. Indeed, the empire’s ancient laws forbade a Sultan’s women from remarrying - but they said nothing about her owning a brothel. A loophole, as far as she was concerned.

Zazie began purging your loyalists while your body was still warm. She emptied the palace guard, summoned every noble's private army, and by nightfall the capital choked with soldiers at every door, every crossing, all while the gutters ran red.

Yet many of yours slipped the noose. Some by the people's mercy, others by foresight or brute power... and soon their rebellions flared across the realm, stoked by the agents you'd planted. The old nobles had promised Zazie armies, but lies come cheap. Just as she'd lied about mercy. Within three days of your death, ten "allied" nobles swung from ropes for withholding troops and gold from the new Sultan and the Sultan-Mother.

Your death tore the realm asunder.You, the regicide, turned inot the martyr. Zazie ruled as the late Sultan's true heir, through steel and terror.

Banners bearing your profile clashed with the golden standards of the throne. The shallow earth grew fat with strong men.

The Boy- Sultan perished at ten. Poison, they said. Then sixty eunuchs and handmaids paid with their heads.

Three years later, Zazie drank the same cup.

After that, no golden-blooded Sultan ever ruled again.

Sharing power with Zazie proved easier than expected. She was clever enough to know what truly threatened your rule and what was merely palace gossip, no matter how scandalous. The former included all the tedious troubles: floods, diplomacy, grain levies, balancing noble and commoner interests. The latter? Those were Zazie's delights, many learned from the late Sultan himself. Yet when the conservative nobles needed appeasing, she played her part flawlessly, as the gilded idol, the mother of the rightful Sultan. She coddled them with sweet lies, letting them dream that once the boy came of age, the realm would return to the empire they remembered. You and Zazie knew better, of course. The realm had changed. But why wake fools from their pleasant dreams?

Eight months after she first took the golden throne heavy with child, the little Sultan was born. Zazie named him Dinarrashan, meaning the Sultan of Golden Coins in the old tongue. Unorthodox, yes. But this was where the advantage of two rulers showed: when the nobles grumbled over the name, whom could they protest to? The woman on the throne and the man beside her had already agreed.

You kept your boundaries with Zazie carefully. In her presence, you bowed, deferential, granting the Sultan-Mother every courtesy. But when truly important matters arose, the ones she cared little for, you made certain the courtiers reported only to you. The more comfortable Zazie grew, the less she thirsted for greater power. And the more stable the realm became.

Two rulers: one a symbol of the new, the other of the old blood and its inherited weight.

And so, for many years, you ruled in balance and good.

Before you placed Zazie upon the throne, she knew nothing of your designs. She thought you merely needed a Sultan's legitimate bloodline as pretext for rule... She was even plotting with the traditionalist nobles to assassinate you, to crown herself, not her child, as true Sultan.

Then you began the Realm of Game. She sensed the trap too late. "Who else holds the Golden rank?" she demanded, before bribing the eunuchs to flee.

You dragged her back. You commanded her to adorn herself as the late Sultan had loved best. Relieved, believing you meant to take her to bed, she emerged nearly bare, skin glistening with rose oil and gold dust, breasts swaying with each step, tiny bells chiming at her nipples. Even the eunuchs stared in awe. Desperate to please her terrifying new Regent, Zazie had never looked more exquisite.

So you hauled her to the palace gates. Before the gathered masses, peddlers, slaves and soldiers, you proclaimed this month's sole Golden Carnality Ticket would be auctioned. The winning bidder could do anything to the Sultan's favorite concubine for a full day.

The crowd roared. None cared how you seized power now. They only knew that you'd torn stars from the sky and let them tread upon celestial flesh. Zazie wept, begging. "The child, the Sultan's heir, your duty is -"

But you whispered, honey-sweet: You refuse the throne to escape its chains. As for who sits upon it... you care not. No Zazie's babe? Another would suffice. So long as the coloring of the skin and hair matched, who'd dare question you? Hadn't you raised a girl from Lady of Delights to Sultan-Mother? How many whores would strangle her bare-handed for that title?

Trembling, wailing, you threw her to the highest bidder.

For years after, there was always a veiled woman on the throne who was claimed to be Zazie. You even provided them with infants to cradle.

Such a considerate Regent, weren't you?

epilogue_2000013.title: Epilogue: Roaming Swordsman
strings: You restored the honor of the fallen royal house, and so the Roaming Swordsman reclaimed his true name - Sirshana. Now, Master Sirshina still drinks himself into oblivion in the taverns, still pinches the backsides of lowborn whores, still brawls and shouts and makes a spectacle of himself. But there’s a lightness to him now, a raw, unfeigned joy. When the wine takes him, he slings an arm around whoever’s nearest and bellows: "That Sultan? That’s my brother! My brother killed my enemies, my dude sits the throne - damn it, this round’s on me! Drink, you bastards, drink!"

You had made too many enemies to even remember when you had wronged this one. That day, your guards seized an old swordsman who had come to kill you - dressed as a merchant, but his skill betrayed him, his eyes burning with fury. "Prince Sirshana is the true Sultan - death to the usurper -" The words died in his throat as your guard’s blade opened it.

You compelled Sirshana, the Roaming Swordsman, to serve in your royal guard. Having seized the throne through regicide, you needed sharper blades around you than the last Sultan ever did...And since you'd restored his house's honor, the homeland nobility finally persuaded him to accept. Now he stands by your throne -yawning, scratching his chest, looking thoroughly bored.But make no mistake: his sword remains as sharp as ever.

After your overthrow, the new ruler - keen to avoid provoking the old loyalists - offered Sirshana title of general. The Swordsman refused. Then he took the envoy's head. And then he and his followers vanished from the realm.

And then he and his followers vanished from the realm.

On the very day you became Regent, your guards caught an old swordsman who tried to assassinate you. He dressed as a merchant, but his skill betrayed him, his eyes burning with fury.

"Prince Sirshana is the true Sultan - death to the usurper -"

The words died in his throat as your guard’s blade opened it.

76 days later, far lesser men who with no loyalty, no cause, no righteousness - finished what the old fool could not.

You restored the honor of the fallen royal house, so the Roaming Swordsman reclaimed his true name - Sirshana. He still haunted the filthy taverns, still took mercenary work, but now there was a fierce, unshakable joy in him.

After your overthrow, yet Zazie - keen to avoid provoking the old loyalists - offered Sirshana title of general. The Swordsman refused. Then he took the envoy’s head.

And then he and his followers vanished from the realm.

You compelled Sirshana, the Roaming Swordsman, to serve in your royal guard. Since you'd also restored his fallen house's honor through the little Sultan's decree, the homeland nobility finally persuaded him to accept. Now he stands by the throne -yawning, scratching his chest, looking thoroughly bored.

But make no mistake: his sword remains as sharp as ever. After your death, he personally slaughtered every eunuch who'd put the leather cord around your throat. To be thorough, he butchered every castrated soul in the palace. Then he cast aside his Iron Guard cloak, gathered his followers, and left the realm forever.

You restored the honor of the fallen royal house, and so the Roaming Swordsman reclaimed his true name - Sirshana.

Now, Master Sirshana still drinks himself into oblivion in the taverns, still pinches the backsides of lowborn whores, still brawls and shouts and makes a spectacle of himself. But there’s a lightness to him now, a raw, unfeigned joy. When the wine takes him, he slings an arm around whoever’s nearest and bellows:

"That Sultan? That’s my brother! My brother killed my enemies, my dude sits the throne - damn it, this round’s on me! Drink, you bastards, drink!”

You'd had to send men to remind him more than once, that you were the Regent, not the Sultan. But the drunken fool had never listened.

You compelled Sirshana, the Roaming Swordsman, to serve in your royal guard. Having seized the throne through regicide, you needed sharper blades around you than the last Sultan ever did...

And since you'd restored his house's honor, the homeland nobility finally persuaded him to accept. Now he stands by your throne -yawning, scratching his chest, looking thoroughly bored.

But make no mistake: his sword remains as sharp as ever.

You wished Sirshana to attend court, yet he refused. When next you sought him, the man had vanished from the capital!

Ever since, tidings reached you from every corner: Sirshana slaughtering bandits in some village, brawling in some noble's domain, bedding whores and fleeing some brothel... Each time he stirred trouble, he invoked your name: "Take your grievances and punishments to the King!"

You could do naught with him. Yet this was not ill, since you had a carefree, merry prince brought smiles to your supporters in the homeland. So long as Sirshana lived, played, and reveled in joy, they knew you to be a king who kept his word.

While you struggled against the lords in the Golden Chamber, Sirshana was of little help, too busy carousing in taverns and brothels, brawling and whoring, then escaping trouble by throwing your name to the wind.

Yet after you painted that golden chamber in blood, Sirshana fell silent. The slain lords had been his staunchest supporters who had once embraced him, given him shelter, shielded him with their lives.

And he knew well: without you, the homeland would never have been restored. What you granted him outweighed all they had offered combined...

Lost in this thorny turmoil, he spoke to you no more, drowning himself instead in revelry, as though pausing but a moment would let grief and fury overtake him.

Years later, drunk, he stumbled into a filthy gutter. Thus did the prince meet his end.

A year later, Sirshana sat upon your throne and faced the same challenge. Since your death, scarcely a week passed without some glory-hungry pit fighter challenging the king. You had named Sirshana a High Lord, after all, making him heir to your crown. And each time, he answered. Each time, he won.

So once more, he strode into the arena, sword in hand.

But this time, he lost. Ten thousand throats roared as the blade opened his. They chanted the victor's name as the man was crowned and your own embroidered cloak draped about his shoulders by simpering maidens, while Sirshana's corpse lay forgotten in the sand.

Such is the way of the "jungle”.

epilogue_2000014.title: Epilogue: Habib
strings: Habib fervently expressed his desire to join your seclusion, but Maggie resolutely insisted him to remain in the capital, tending to your Guesthouse. Now, every week, he sends the house's earnings along with a letter. They were unbearably long, unnecessarily detailed, and utterly devoid of useful information.

Habib returned to your homeland by Maggie's design. When you questioned her, she merely smiled and shook her head. "My sweet Sultan, my husband, the way Habib looks at me is not the gaze of a servant to his master. Could you not tell? Had I kept him by my side, sooner or later he would have grown bold, and then you would have had no choice but to kill him." She sighed, "And what a waste that would have been to lose the finest cook in all the realm." At least, in your homeland, Habib still sends his spiced jerky and preserved fruits, as rich and perfect as ever.

Habib is now the palace chef.

Everyone eagerly anticipates your banquets, and even the wealthiest Nobles admit that nowhere compares to the new Sultan [player.name]'s feast. Novel dishes, skilled techniques, and richly scented spices make people's mouths water with just a mention.

However, Maggie seems less fond of Habib than before, and she also found a female palace chef for the ladies' meals... Although, it's a small matter and nothing that needs your concern.
At Maggie's bidding, Habib now serves in the kitchens of highborn ladies, where his dishes earn lavish praise. Yet even in another's employ, he still sends Maggie's favored candied fruits and dishes.

After your fall, Habib tried to take Maggie away, but she refused.

They found his body in a dry well beneath the palace. Suicide, they said.

Habib remained by your side, but as Maggie withered day by day, so too did he.

You found it amusing: this man who worshipped Maggie as a goddess, forced to watch you cage her in a harem that choked her spirit…… The suffering of others watered your happiness like spring rain.

"The Sultan's own cook feeds us now”, the words spread faster than wildfire. Soon Habib toiled from dawn till dusk, while volunteers swarmed so thick that men began queuing before first light.

epilogue_2000019.title: Epilogue: Jenna
strings: Jenna crafted a glorious jewel inspired by dragon slaying, Yet the gemstone eyes were lost to the tides of war.

Your council decreed a new path to nobility: any man or woman who mastered a craft might earn lands and title.

Jenna rose by this measure. Her jewel-house in the capital was renowned, its works unmatched in skill or artistry. Now styled "Lady Jenna", she kept a replica of the ruby coronet in her shop's place of pride: the very circlet you had worn as Vizier when you and Nawfal took the throne.

epilogue_2000021.title: Epilogue: Iman
strings: Iman still serves the Purist. To your coronation, he offered only bloodly blessings without any words. Yet this silence sat better upon the throne than the priests' fawning madness... or so you chose to believe.

Iman still serves the Purist. He has grown happier of late, his tongue looser than before. At your coronation, he offered blessings aplenty. "I must particularly praise the Sultan's mercy and kindness," he said, "and that heart which holds such magnificent love – so vast it may embrace multitudes. Truly, this is a miracle worthy of divine descent."

Iman came when you called. His silent presence at your side convinced the realm the Purist had chosen you, and your rule prospered. Yet fate's knife found your belly soon enough. As your life bled away, Iman called upon the purest words of power. In a blaze of sacred light, your wounds knit whole. That very night, he died. They say his last whisper was: "Ah... good. I have waited too long."

Iman came when you called. Only after the sycophants had withdrawn, when you first slumped wearily upon the gilded throne, did he approach. Taking your hand and Maggie's in his own, he leaned close to her ear, and spoke. The pure word surged through Maggie, mending what was broken within. Yet as her wounds closed, Iman's back split open, flesh parting to reveal glistening bone. Still, he smiled: "Necessary thanks," he whispered. "You cannot know what you did for me... After your death, Iman, the High Priest of the Purist delivered a condemning oracle. The Purist spoke through him to curse Zazie - usurper, murderer of their most favored servant.

Then one night, not long after the prophecy, Iman was found dead in his chambers. Upon his back gaped a single, terrible wound, as though the gods themselves had scourged a lying prophet.

The Purist Order loathed the resurgent Star-Souled cults that rose with your restoration. So when you plotted to purge those old nobles who sought to leash you, Iman lent his aid.

Thanks to him, you stalled their levies without spending a drop of royal blood. Thanks to the Purist's oracles, you weathered the vengeful fury of the enraged Star-Souleds.

epilogue_2000022.title: Epilogue: Badriyyah
strings: Badriyyah still rules the Cult. She never speaks of knowing you. Whispers say she fears such tidings would shatter the already fractured minds of her followers.

Soon after your coronation, a crude gift was presented that wrapped in blood-slick pelts and bristling with garish blooms. The protocol minister could not tell whether it was curse or blessing. Inside, you found a sigil. A many-eyed god stared back from its surface. On its reverse, words were carved: "Before you need my aid, this will serve." And serve it did. Once... twice... you wielded it, and watched as foes were dragged into the void. So far, at least, you have not needed Badriyyah herself.

What exactly could Badriyyah do in your palace? Truth be told, you weren’t entirely sure and neither was she, for that matter. But both of you agreed: having the high priestess of the Cult lounging in the Sultan’s court was simply too amusing to pass up. She came every day, brewing strange elixirs before your golden throne, or skinning sacrificial offerings (animals, thankfully) in full view of scandalized noblewomen. Then, one day, she stopped appearing. When you sent enforcers to inquire, her followers could only say she had spoken of summoning a "great demon lord", then vanished inside the Cult’s caverns. Only a pile of robes remained before the altar. The cultist who relayed this news sounded almost envious: "Badriyyah found a cause worthy of her devotion!"

The moralists, of course, had their own interpretation: "The Sultan keeps her here as a reminder that power often reeks of blood and filth." That one had made the two of you laugh for days.

After your coronation, Badriyyah no longer visited. Mortal kings held little interest for her.But you met often after your death. She and her cultists stole your body in the dead of night. Now, whenever Badriyyah comes to gather blossoms for her sacred inks, she brings a flask of liquor, pouring it slowly into the earth as she murmurs words too soft for anyone else to hear. No one knows what secrets she whispers to your grave.

epilogue_2000054.title: Epilogue: Jabal
strings: Jabal and Adila came to honor your coronation, then set forth together to seek greater perils. Like true companions, they fought side by side, polished their armor together, and raised cups in triumph. Years later, Adila and Jabal slew the monstrous octopus that lurked in the distant western seas... Now, a fifth of all newborns in the capital bear the names "Adila" and "Jabal", and their deeds are sung in ballads across the realm.

Adila and Jabal set forth in search of greater prey. "If we cannot slay a dragon," Adila told you before their departure, "then we shall settle for something nearly as formidable." Her husband nodded in grim agreement. "We mean to test our steel against the great octopus of the western seas, the beast that claims a hundred ships each year. Its debt of blood has come due." You wished them fair winds.

Of course the Dragonslayers remained at court. The mere presence of Adila and Jabal lent your reign legitimacy! Each dawn found the legendary couple drilling troops in the palace yards. Every soldier bowed deeply when they passed - those fortunate enough to earn even a cursory fighting lesson treasured it like dragonbone. Yet you knew their secret pact: They would stay but a few years to steady your throne. After that? The western seas called. Rumor spoke of a giant octopus there worth killing.

You kept Adila and Jabal in the Court. These two valiant warriors are sure to help you secure your throne. On the night the appointment was announced, they both came to find you..."Three years, we'll act as good Generals for you for three years, how about it?" Jabal suggested, then Adila gave a strong smack to his head, "Three years is too long—two years! [player.name], two years should be enough for you to secure the Sultan's position; after two years we will go to kill the giant octopus because if we didn't succeed in killing the big lizard, we have to kill some other big game!" You haggled down to two and a half years and then agreed to their terms.

Jabal remained unchanged by the shifting of crowns. He still chased the thrill of the hunt and the clamor of battle. Though he held no title in your new court, the old general always appeared when steel was needed. When the coup against you was finally crushed, they found his body in the streets. He lay before a mound of at least thirty slain rebels, as though he had fought alone to bar their path to the palace. To the last, he remained a proud and mighty Iron Guard.

You kept Jabal as your general, letting his blade remain unsheathed in the halls of the Lapis Lazuli Court. When the next rebellion came, he gathered his men and told them: "A true warrior fights for a worthy ruler unto death, for what greater honor can a master bestow than a cause worth dying for?" They died in the chaos of defending your palace, with proud and honor.

Sometimes, he would come to the palace with a skin of wine, and you would drink together, speaking of the Sultan's games. "Is it better now, Your Majesty?" He squinted at you through the haze of liquor. "Being Sultan... or being the Sultan's man? Which is the sweeter poison?" You could only answer with a bitter smile and another poured cup.
