"Three years, we'll act as good Generals for you for three years, how about it?" Jabal suggested, then Adila gave a strong smack to his head, "Three years is too long—two years! [player.name], two years should be enough for you to secure the Sultan's position; after two years we will go to kill the giant octopus because if we didn't succeed in killing the big lizard, we have to kill some other big game!"

You haggled down to two and a half years and then agreed to their terms.

Jabal and Adila came to congratulate you for winning the Sultan's game in your own way., then set forth together to seek greater perils. Like true companions, they fought side by side, polished their armor together, and raised cups in triumph.

They never returned. Likely, to this day, they still don't know you've fallen... But perhaps that's for the best. Heroes always meet again in the great dream beyond.

On the day you were struck down, Jabal was hunting a great boar. When the breathless messenger came bearing news of your death, the beast's last shuddering breath left its body at that very moment.

He came charging back to camp with his boar-bloodied blade, but it was too late. There was nothing left to save.

Days later, they hanged Jabal for trying to slit the throat of Sadani, the Regent.

Jabal and Adila came to congratulate you for winning the Sultan's game in your own way., then set forth together to seek greater perils. Like true companions, they fought side by side, polished their armor together, and raised cups in triumph.

They never returned.

Jabal remained unchanged by the shifting of crowns. He still chased the thrill of the hunt and the clamor of battle. Though he held no title in your new court, the old general always appeared when steel was needed.

When the coup against you was finally crushed, they found his body in the streets. He lay before a mound of at least thirty slain rebels, as though he had fought alone to bar their path to the palace.

To the last, he remained a proud and mighty Iron Guard.

You kept Jabal as your general, letting his blade remain unsheathed in the halls of the Lapis Lazuli Court.

When the next rebellion came, he gathered his men and told them: "A true warrior fights for a worthy ruler unto death, for what greater honor can a master bestow than a cause worth dying for?"

They died in the chaos of defending your palace, with proud and honor.

Jabal and Adila came to honor your coronation, then set forth together to seek greater perils. Like true companions, they fought side by side, polished their armor together, and raised cups in triumph.

They never returned.

Jabal remained unchanged by the shifting of crowns. He still chased the thrill of the hunt and the clamor of battle. Though he held no title in your new court, the old general always appeared when steel was needed.

After your fall, they found his body in the streets, and surrounded by the corpses of at least a dozen royal guards. In death, he had bought precious time for those still loyal to you to escape.

To the last, he remained a proud and mighty Iron Guard.

You kept Jabal as your general, letting his blade remain unsheathed in the halls of the Lapis Lazuli Court.

When Zazie began purging the palace, Jabal gathered his men and told them: "A true warrior fights for a worthy ruler unto death, for what greater honor can a master bestow than a cause worth dying for?"

They died in the chaos of defending your palace, with proud and honor.

Adila and Jabal set forth in search of greater prey.

"If we cannot slay a dragon," Adila told you before their departure, "then we shall settle for something nearly as formidable." Her husband nodded in grim agreement. "We mean to test our steel against the great octopus of the western seas, the beast that claims a hundred ships each year. Its debt of blood has come due."

Long after they'd gone, Zazie wore a pensive look for days. "So that's how a marriage can be," she mused. "No scheming, no clawing for dominance... neither stronger nor weaker. Fascinating. But not for me."

With a toss of her head, she cast the thought aside and went hunting fresher sport.

Of course the Dragonslayers remained at court. The mere presence of Adila and Jabal lent you and Zazie's reign legitimacy!

Each dawn found the legendary couple drilling troops in the palace yards. Every soldier bowed deeply when they passed - those fortunate enough to earn even a cursory fighting lesson treasured it like dragonbone.

Yet you knew their secret pact: They would stay but a few years to steady your throne. After that? The western seas called. Rumor spoke of a giant octopus there worth killing.

You kept Adila and Jabal in the Court. Their prominent family background will surely help secure your throne. Moreover, you want to show off your influence over these two valiant warriors before Zazie.

On the night the appointment was announced, they both came to find you...

"Three years, we'll act as good Generals for you for three years, how about it?" Jabal suggested, then Adila gave a strong smack to his head, "Three years is too long—two years! [player.name], two years should be enough for you to secure the Sultan's position; after two years we will go to kill the giant octopus, because if we didn't succeed in the killing of the big lizard, we have to kill some other big game!"

You haggled down to two and a half years and then agreed to their terms.

Jabal took the throne from Adila. His reign lasted four years, until a mortal duel left him bleeding out, though not before he dragged his killer down with him. Three days later, he died in his palace chambers.

The realm passed then to the great gladiator. No messenger's cry nor sigil's proclamation was needed. People simply knew where power flowed. Just as every ape in the jungle, every tree in the forest knows the law of tooth and claw.

Jabal stood among the staunchest supporters of King Sirshana. Even without his grievances against the previous Sultan, this new ruler simply suited him too well.

He remained the General of the court, yet spent more hours in the fighting pits than before you or Sirshana. Or perhaps that wasn't entirely true, for Sirshana himself was rarely in the palace either. The two often slipped away to the arenas together, critiquing gladiators' techniques, showering victors with gold, even sharing drinks with the most skilled fighters. What a strange and wondrous land this was, where a king and his general raised cups to bloodstained slaves, toasting their health!

After Sirshana's death, Jabal vanished for a long while. When he finally returned, he knelt before you and spoke words no one expected:"I have thought long on this, your Majesty... and I beg you, close the fighting pits. For good."

His voice was rough with grief. "The thought of soft-bellied men who've never held a shield daring to judge King Sirshana's battles... it sickens me. I want no more of it."

You granted his request.

When you took the throne, Adila and Jabal stood at your sides, heads held high with pride and satisfaction.

But that pride lasted only a few short months. Soon enough, the fierce warrior couple came before you with their minds set: they would hunt greater prey.

"A pity you're Sultan now and can't go where you please," they said, grinning. "So you'll just have to wait on your throne for our tales of battle! Ha! We'll raise hell in your name!"

They left laughing. Truth be told, you couldn't help but feel a pang of regret... To hunt the great leviathans of the western seas, now that would have been a sight to see.

Adila and Jabal followed you through every campaign and hunting. After each conquest, it was they who bore the trophies back to the capital, be it heads, tails, or fangs, depending on which part of the prey your forces had shattered first, to proclaim your glory far and wide.

People say your court grew so crammed with these grim trophies that men could scarcely find room to stand.

Adila and Jabal left the realm before your madness took full hold.

You breathed a sigh of relief.

They occasionally send trophies to the empire, each bearing your name; sometimes massive horns, other times crystalline bones vast as siege towers. Perhaps they hope these grim gifts might summon back the [player.name] they once knew: the one who laughed and cursed and fought beside them, the friend who died when the "Dragon-Slaying Sultan" took his place.

Jabal took your naming of Adila as Vizier with conflicted emotions, discontent warring against pride. The discontent came easy: his fierce and steadfast wife could no longer ride at his side to hunt what prey they pleased. Yet the pride ran deeper, a swelling tide in his chest that Adilai deserved every honor under the sun!

Half year into her tenure, she begged three months' leave. With it, she and Jabal crossed into the neighboring realm, shattered the Yeti King that plagued its people, and bore back its monstrous foot as tribute... mercifully dried and cured.

Thereafter, every few years saw them vanish on such ventures. Their trophies mounted, each new claw or fang a fresh goad to your restlessness. Curse this damned Sultan's crown! How you longed to ride with them, if only duty's chains did not bind you so.

As your Vizier, Adila grew sickened by your butchery. She told you plainly: "A head taken by another's sword does not count. No matter how many fall, it earns you no warrior's glory."

In time, she gave up on you entirely. She left your realm with Jabal at her side, the first Vizier who fled her own Sultan's court.

You breathed a sigh of relief.

They occasionally send trophies to the empire, each bearing your name; sometimes massive horns, other times crystalline bones vast as siege towers. Perhaps they hope these grim gifts might summon back the [player.name] they once knew: the one who laughed and cursed and fought beside them, the friend who died when the "Dragon-Slaying Sultan" took his place.

Jabal once stood before the court and proposed his vision: an adventurers' guild to draw quests from across the realm. Mocking laughter answered him, so you had every laughing man put to the sword.

At first, Jabal found grim satisfaction in it. Then came silence.

Weeks later, he and Adila left your realm behind.

They occasionally send trophies to the empire, each bearing your name; sometimes massive horns, other times crystalline bones vast as siege towers. Perhaps they hope these grim gifts might summon back the [player.name] they once knew: the one who laughed and cursed and fought beside them, the friend who died when the "Dragon-Slaying Sultan" took his place.

epilogue_2000055.title: Epilogue: Nayla
strings: Nayla had been furious when you left the court. She had expected you to stay as the Sultan, to make her the hostess of your harem. Her rage was so precise, so venomous, that she even sent assassins after Maggie... Jealousy is a poison that twists the soul. In the end, you quietly called upon old friends...Now, she is in permanent silence.

To Nayla, you were different - not just for your skills between the sheets - ahem - not just for your tenderness, but because of that old woman you once tended to, the closest thing to light she'd ever known. When you left, she spoke not a word. You never saw each other again.

Nayla was delighted with her new appointment - a sentiment shared by absolutely no one else. She took to parading through the halls daily, adorned in silks and smirks. This, of course, was the extent of her understanding of "politics." And naturally, no one had any intention of enlightening her further.

Nayla had been furious when you left the court. Though do not mistake her rage for anything as tender as heartbreak. She had expected you to stay as the Sultan, to make her the hostess of your harem. Instead, you tossed power into the gutter - Pathetic. Weak. A Failure! Now, when your name is spoken, she doesn’t even bother to scoff, less than a discarded shoe.

Nayla was ecstatic about your new regime. At last, she reigned as the empire's most exalted woman! To her, wielding power directly was a tedious chore; far sweeter was to leech upon it, to twist authority she never earned into a weapon against all who dared cross her.

And so, through venom and vicious scheming, she clawed her way to dominance in your harem. None could rival her - not your wife, not the former Sultan's concubines -. She broke them all, one by one, until the very air of the palace trembled at her whim.

By the time you finally snapped and ordered her death, she had already amassed obscene riches in your name. Her bed was solid gold - "For the sultan must rest in splendor!" Her silks were the finest woven - "How else to please His Majesty's eye?" Her perfumes cost more than gold -"For the Sultan catch a whiff of pleasure!" And the promises she made, whispering to sycophants that she alone could sway your ear, brazenly boasting that you owed her for your throne... Enough is enough. You ordered her death. You should have done it years ago.

Nayla had been surprised by your ascension to Sultan. Rumors reached your ears about how she’d muttered: "If I’d known he’d actually claw his way to the throne, I’d have bothered more. Who’d have thought a man with, well... kindness could manage it?".

Nayla was ecstatic about your new regime. At last, she reigned as the empire's most exalted woman! To her, wielding power directly was a tedious chore; far sweeter was to leech upon it, to twist authority she never earned into a weapon against all who dared cross her. And your court rotted faster for it. When you were assassinated and the usurpers found her, she shouted:"I shall serve the new king with such devotion - "The sword fell while her head kept speaking.

After your death, people scrambled to list your crimes - most fabricated, some exaggerated, a very few you'd actually committed. When the ever-growing scroll reached Nayla, she merely signed her name. No words. No accusations. Then she left the capital. No one ever saw her again.

Nayla left you soon after arriving China. Or rather, she found men fancier, stronger, richer... They say she became a prince's shadow advisor, tending to his unspeakable needs, whispering schemes of succession into his ear. You never had the chance to ask her if it was true.

Even Nayla declared you "the fiercest lover" she'd ever slept with To honor your memory, she commissioned a golden dildo, wrought in your exact likeness. The artisans marveled at its proportions, making people wonder if she was the fiercest one instead.

After your death, Nayla served three more Sultans in turn. Her skill, beauty, and cunning pleased each ruler well enough, not that she feared time's touch, for all three combined sat the throne less than five years.

When the last Sultan sensed his impending downfall, he took Nayla's head, lest his favorite use tales of his bedchamber prowess to charm yet another successor. She had, after all, done so before.

And the promises she made, whispering to sycophants that she alone could sway your ear, brazenly boasting that you owed her for your throne...

Enough is enough. You ordered her death. You should have done it years ago.

Nayla seethed at your choice. In her eyes, you should have claimed the Sultan's thronet, then she would reign as the empire's most exalted woman! That dry, charmless Sadani could never compare to her!

Not long after birthing the new Sultan, Sadani sent you a letter dripping with courtesy... and two concubines as gifts. Nayla saw this as nothing less than open war. Enraged, she redoubled her venomous assaults against Sadani - no, now the Queen Mother Sadarni - until one night, those very concubines found their moment and cast her down a well.

They knelt before you, begging mercy. "She would have slain us," they pleaded, "we but defended ourselves." They even offered their own lives to atone for your loss.

Suddenly you understood Sadani's message: others schemed for her, others killed for her... and she wished you to know it.

You sent the concubines back unharmed.

Nayla fancied herself among the empire's most exalted women now. Though Sadani, who styled as the Queen Mother, made no secret of her disdain, Nayla still haunted the royal court with increasing frequency after Sadani bore a son, the future Sultan.

Most expected Nayla to stir trouble, like pinching the royal heir, pilfering the Queen Mother's jewels, or picking fights with her ladies. Yet instead, she would often sit transfixed, watching the babe suckle at his mother's breast. In those moments, she fell silent, her eyes glistening, almost unrecognizable. When Sadani inevitably dismissed her with impatience, Nayla would startle as if waking from a dream, murmur apologies, leave behind some lavish gift, and retreat in haste.

"Perhaps even she has some goodness left," they said. "Even Nayla can be moved."

Nayla despised what this realm had become. She craved a Sultan who would shower her with power, a man bewitched by her charms, a ruler who'd make her the realm's most exalted woman!

So she chose a particularly dim-witted noble with a drop of royal blood, one who'd sworn to crown her queen should he take the throne. She emptied her pockets, called in favors from every former lover, and struck when your regency stood most vulnerable.

She fought better than expected indeed, but only slightly better. Within three days the rebellion was crushed. The would-be Sultan, Nayla, and three dozen traitorous nobles swung from the tallest tree. That night, ravens and foxes came from miles around to feast. What a most magnificent banquet.

Nayla had been surprised by your ascension to Regent. Rumors reached your ears about how she’d muttered: "If I’d known he’d actually claw his way to the throne, I’d have bothered more. Who’d have thought a man with, well... kindness could manage it?".

After your death, people scrambled to list your crimes - most fabricated, some exaggerated, a very few you'd actually committed. When the ever-growing scroll reached Nayla, she signed no words.

Then she left the capital. No one ever saw her again.

Nayla had been surprised by your ascension to Regent. Rumors reached your ears about how she’d muttered: "If I’d known he’d actually claw his way to the throne, I’d have bothered more. I could've borne his kid and claimed it as the Sultan's heir! Who’d have thought a man with, well... kindness could manage it?"

Nayla was ecstatic about your new regime. At last, she reigned as the empire's most exalted woman!

To her, wielding power directly was a tedious chore; far sweeter was to leech upon it, to twist authority she never earned into a weapon against all who dared cross her. And your court rotted faster for it.

When you were assassinated and the usurpers found her, she shouted:"I shall serve you with such devotion - "The sword fell while her head kept speaking.

Nayla had simply assumed you would invite her into your harem, to crown her the empire's most exalted woman, only for you to refuse the Sultan's crown itself! She finally left with great anger. From then on, she spat venom at every opportunity.

When you were assassinated, as your lifeless body lay upon the square, she laughed, yet did not notice the usurper's soldiers turning toward her. She did not see the noose being readied.

Her corpse fed the rats of the pauper's graveyard.

Nayla seethed with grievances against you. She believed you should have claimed the Sultan's throne for yourself, then she would reign as queen! Never mind that the empire recognized no such title, nor cared she for noble factions, reformists, or political balances. She desired only to be the realm's most exalted woman.

Still, "the Regent's Lady" proved better than nothing. She wielded the title like a whip, amassing treasures in your name. She host lavish feasts where every guest seeking your favor was compelled to bring tribute, including exotic rose elixirs, hummingbird rings set with cats' eyes, moonstone necklaces that shimmered like captured stars... The richer Nayla's coffers grew, the fouler your reputation became.

In the little Sultan's third year, Nayla died in a country manor. That morning she had spoken of taking the waters with noble ladies, yet they found her sprawled beside two dead men of unknown origin.

The realm buzzed with theories. Had her pleasures grown too wild? Had she sampled some exotic poison for thrill? All agreed on this much: you were the long-suffering victim, and she the wanton harlot who squandered your kindness.

Good, you thought. This meant you'd chosen the perfect moment to remove her.

Some expected Nayla to wield your name, the Regent's name, like a bludgeon, to carve her influence through the court. Yet the vain lady proved strangely subdued.

Only in rare moments did she speak of it.

"You know..." she mused once, "I've been thinking how a life may turn on the smallest of things. A mere maid, forgotten by history... or well, who can say?" She shook her head, sudden irritation flashing. "But no matter, I'm bored of it. Must you press so? Keep asking, and I'll demand that golden bed you owe me!"

Nayla had simply assumed you would invite her into your harem, to crown her the empire's most exalted woman. You never understood why she believed this, but when you raised up that other woman and her whelp instead, her fury knew no bounds.

She poisoned every gathering with venomous tongues, whispering that you bedded Sadani and raised her child out of lust rather than duty...

When they found her corpse in her manse some month later, you and Sadani shared a silence thicker than palace walls. Some truths need never be spoken.

When the palace guards came for Nayla after your assassination, she shrieked to the last: "I'll serve the new Sultan! I'll wait for him to come of age!”

Her lips still formed those words even as the blade fell.

When Zazie's men came for Nayla and asked of her connection to you, the vain fool couldn't resist boasting. "Of course we were acquainted," she declared, "He called me the finest woman he'd ever known!"

They made sure those were the last words her pretty head would utter.

When Nayla boasted for the third time that she was fairer than the Sultan's mother, Zazie finally summoned you.

You stood in silence, until at last she gave a nod. "My apologies," she said. You understood. That evening, you made certain to return home late.

It was for the best. Watching the woman you'd wed get a knife through her ribs would have stirred... unnecessary feelings. Now, arriving just in time to see her shrouded corpse, the timing was perfect.

Nayla showed little interest in your role as Regent. "What's the point of being Regent when you're not Sultan?" she'd scoff whenever you asked.

Yet one day, when you attended court with her before Zazie and the little Sultan, a wet nurse knelt trembling: her husband forbade her to serve, claiming no woman should bare her breasts before men not her own.

“Tell him to go to hell, or you will send him," Nayla's voice cut like a whip, startling the hall. “I'm the Regent's wife. Tell him I commanded it."

After that, the wet nurse stayed. And Zazie... well, she looked upon Nayla with new eyes.

Nayla seemed genuinely surprised you hadn't claimed the throne for yourself. "What a strange man," she was heard complaining to others. "Passing up the throne for someone else to take! Though... perhaps it's better for the realm this way. Less bloodshed. That's just like him - always thinking of others. I can't stand such bleeding hearts."

Nayla would never trail after you like some common women. How could she sleep without her sandalwood bed with gilded feet?

And she cared not a whit about remaining in the capital, being worshipped as "the Sultan's woman," basking in flattery and tribute. "The best husband is the Sultan," she'd often laugh, "and the best Sultan is one who stays away!"

Of course, when words reached you years later that she'd died in her manse with her chambers picked clean, you found you scarce mourned at all.

Nayla would never trail after you like some common women. How could she sleep without her sandalwood bed with gilded feet?

So she demanded a divorce. A woman dared to divorce the great Dragon-slaying Sultan! But you saw no reason to refuse it, so you just let her go.

After that... you never heard of her again.

epilogue_2000056.title: Epilogue: Qais
strings:
Qais roared his disapproval of your butchery, just as he'd done with the last Sultan.

The man was too loud by half, so you threw him in the black cells, as the last Sultan had done.

But this time... there was no one to play the rescuer. So he died there in the dark.

epilogue_2000057.title: Epilogue: Jawad
strings: Jawad never missed a chance to brag about how he once managed your household and aided your inventions. Even his first betrayal became part of the tale, telling the traitor redeemed, the grudge dissolved like morning frost.

epilogue_2000061.title: Epilogue: Adila
strings:
Adila became the pride of her bloodline, not just because she dared to challenge the dragon and forced the beast to flee in disgrace, but also because she's a friend of the reigning Sultan. That she now walks as the Sultan's confidant only seals her triumph. The matriarchs nod in grim approval - mother, grandmother, aunts - all whispering the same verdict: "She could rise no higher."

From that day forth, every firstborn daughter of the house has borne the name "Adila".

That she now walks as the Sultan's confidant only seals her triumph. The matriarchs nod in grim approval - mother, grandmother, aunts - all whispering the same verdict: "She could rise no higher."

From that day forth, every firstborn daughter of the house has borne the name "Adila".

She has since set out to roam the world, seeking prey worthy of her might. Yet, out of gratitude to you, she has sworn to return every three years and present the skull of her latest kill to you, her Sultan - if only to silence, for a time, the buzzing nobles who swarm like flies around the throne. Each time she returns, she shakes her head at your plight. She claps you on the shoulder (with far too much force, though you endure it with dignity) and booms: "You toiled and bled for this? To sit in a gilded cage and listen to fools bicker? Bah! What nonsense! Come with me instead! let's hunt something real. The Yeti King of the Frostpeaks awaits!" And oh, how you wish you could.

The dragon still breathes, yet Adila's valor sent ripples through the realm. Her acceptance of your appointment and joining your court - lent strength to your rule. However, Adila was ill-suited for courtly service. She endured the ceremonies for ten days before erupting in fury. "Let me hunt the dragon instead! Anything is better than this drudgery!"

The noble opponents sneered, "See how the Sultan wastes his favor on one who refuses to kneel!" But you laughed, then released her. Now she roams free, seeking greater prey. If you could not escape your gilded cage, then at least Adila's fiery heart should never be caged.

By some twist of fate, Adila found herself following you to China, where new "dragons" awaited! Or so she fervently believed. Poring over ancient texts, she became convinced that those "dragons" of different colors took turns steering this empire's destiny. Yet having already faced one dragon, she declared this hunt "not mine to take". "Let the next generation have their glory," she reasoned. "A century hence, when rival dragons clash and mortals may strike. That will be their hour." So instead, she turned to forging legacy. She took on disciples. She bore children - all daughters...

Adila, the hero who drove back the dragons, left the realm in search of greater prey after your coronation.

When she returned, she found a stranger upon the throne. First came shock, then came tears. When the weeping ended, she scornfully cast down the blade the new Sultan gifted her, along with the decree naming her Iron Guard, and stomped upon them. Then she turned her back on the court... and never returned.

A handmaiden who witnessed it all later swore the new Sultan shrieked for his guards to strike down the insolent woman. But the guards pretended not to hear. What fool would raise steel against a Dragonslayer?

You welcomed Adila, the Dragonslayer into your court, making her one of your Iron Guards.

She proved the fiercest of them all, even when an enemy's poisoned arrow pierced her throat, she tore it out and slew three more assassins with the bloody shaft before finally falling.

After her death, the women of her house donned steel and rode for vengeance. They slaughtered hundreds of rebel soldiers in the capital before withdrawing to their lands, raising towering walls and digging impassable moats. For generations thereafter, their fortress remained the most stubborn thorn in every ruler's side, a nest of rebellion that no crown could ever purge.

Adila, the Dragonslayer, neither approved nor condemned your deeds.

Many gathered at her family's gates, begging her to stand against the tyrant. Tyrant they said! As if you were anything but a man who loved his games! Yet Adila kept her silence.

epilogue_2000062.title: Epilogue: Fatuna
strings: Fatuna and Zaki followed you to the hermitage, purchasing a grand estate nearby. Zaki became the local master's right hand, while Fatuna tended the gardens with Maggie, sipping tea among the blossoms. When Zaki returned early from his duties, he would join you for conversation. The mother and son were content for the peaceful life.

The new regime’s favored were summoned to the capital. Fatuna would not leave Maggie, nor Zaki abandon you, yet they neither had a choice. You regularly received lavish gifts from them in the capital, though Maggie always wrote back urging "Don't send such extravagant gifts”. But the mother and son apparently ignored her words.

Fatuna and Zaki came to your hermitage, living with you within your halls. When the local master learned Zaki was your foster son, he offered the boy a place at his side, a foothold in the game of favors and parchment. Maggie and Fatuna stitched his entire outfit themselves. Now the women tend the gardens, sipping tea among the blossoms. Zaki toiled over the master's business without respite. He would not shame his father through sloth. The mother and son were content for the peaceful life.

You secured Fatuna a title at court, though her heart ached to leave Zaki, Maggie, and you most of all. Yet she understood your design, and so bore the parting without complaint.

Now she stands among your staunchest allies before the new Sultan's throne. Her melancholy grace has won her admirers. When pressed with questions she cannot answer, a single tear begins the tale of her first husband's death, and this second separation... until even the most persistent critic relents.

Zaki rode between your hermitage and the capital, as messenger, but more of an eager apprentice. His mother watched, willing him to take her place so she might retreat at last. She had heard of Maggie's garden, and her heart had flown there in her every dream.

You secured Zaki a title at court,, and though Fatuna swelled with pride, her joy was laced with grief. As your wife, she would accompany you to the hermitage, her heart already dancing through Maggie's gardens. But as a mother... the day had come to leave her son behind. Though she'd known this parting would come, still the tears fell silently.

Zaki proved worthy. As your foster son, he became your fiercest voice in the royal court. At the faintest whisper against your quiet exile, he would bare his teeth like a direwolf, relentless until the threat retreated. You knew of the letters passing between the mother and son. The boy's political cunning bore his mother's careful script, each word another stitch in the tapestry of his education.

Fatuna and Zaki remained in the capital. After what happened with Maggie, Fatuna scarcely spoke to you at all, and when Zaki sought conversation, he had to steal moments away from his stern mother. Their comfortable, prosperous life carried on. The young man slipping away to visit you when he could, while his mother hung Maggie's portrait in their lavish mansion.

Those elevated by the new regime remained in the capital. Zaki had wished to follow you into seclusion, but Fatuna would not allow it.

"Think about Maggie, my boy," she said it to your face, "He is no longer a man worth following." Reluctantly, Zaki obeyed his mother. Yet still the ravens came, bearing his letters full of courtly trifles and whispered intrigues.

Fatuna and Zaki remained your most steadfast supporters, and Zaki most of all. The young noble made it his mission to sing the new Sultan's praises in every ear, ensuring no ill word of you could be spoken unchallenged. You often suspected gold from his own coffers had silenced certain inconvenient voices among your detractors, yet lacking proof and you did not care...

Meanwhile, Fatuna often sought Maggie’s company where they would take their ease in the old rose garden, steeping freshly plucked petals into pomegranate tea and enjoying desserts. The two noblewomen would while away entire afternoons in pleasant discourse.

Fatuna and Zaki remained your most steadfast supporters, and Zaki most of all. The young noble made it his mission to sing the new Sultan's praises in every ear, ensuring no ill word of you could be spoken unchallenged. You often suspected gold from his own coffers had silenced certain inconvenient voices among your detractors, yet lacking proof and you did not care...

Meanwhile, Fatuna and Maggie became dearest companion. They would take their ease in the old rose garden, steeping freshly plucked petals into pomegranate tea and enjoying desserts. The two most noble women in the realm would while away entire afternoons in pleasant discourse.

Zaki bored his new courtly burdens with fierce pride, laboring tirelessly lest he prove unworthy of your trust. Meanwhile, Fatuna's lavish gifts flowed into the palace like a river of gold. Maggie pleaded with you more than once to command her to cease such offerings, but you saw no reason to deny a mother’s right to honor her son's ascent. The backing of this wealthy, ancient house served your fledgling reign well.

Zaki bored his new courtly burdens with fierce pride, laboring tirelessly lest he prove unworthy of your trust.Meanwhile, Fatuna had departed the capital, leaving her son's side. No protest passed her lips - what fool would openly question the Sultan's will? Yet you knew her thoughts lingered on Maggie's fate. However, Zaki's fervent loyalty more than balanced his mother's icy glances.

Fatuna and Zaki remained your most steadfast supporters, and Zaki most of all. The young master made it his mission to sing the new Sultan's praises in every ear, ensuring no ill word of you could be spoken unchallenged. 

But when news of your assassination reached them, they fell to shock and despair. Days later, someone found Fatuna's body swaying from the rafters of her manor. Her final words were etched in grief: "The new sun has fallen. My life has been lived on brittle ice, and I cannot endure another turn of the wheel, another age of chaos... I am weary. Let me go. And do not seek my son. This is my last plea." 

They tried, of course. But Zaki was already gone. He fled across the sea with chests of gold, vanishing into the distant land. There, he paid the finest bards and poets to weave your tale into song. Ballads of your glory and tragedy still echoes in taverns and halls to this day.

Fatuna and Zaki remained your most steadfast supporters, knowing well the struggle of bending nobles to your will, and so they came often, bearing gifts. 

They brought you comfort - and to Maggie, they were dearest guests. They would take their ease in the old rose garden, steeping freshly plucked petals into pomegranate tea, giggling like girls as they fussed over the balance of tart and sweet. Sometimes it turned too sharp.They winced, then laughed, spilling tea on costly silks. But their joy in that moment was worth more than gold. 

Zaki lingers at your ear, buzzing with rumors and grand plans for the realm. You recognized the hollow words nobles planted in him, but you let him speak. Let him believe effort can change the world. Such delusions were the right of the young.

Fatuna and Zaki remained your most steadfast supporters, and Zaki most of all. The young master made it his mission to sing the new Sultan's praises in every ear, ensuring no ill word of you could be spoken unchallenged. You often suspected gold from his own coffers had silenced certain inconvenient voices among your detractors, yet lacking proof and you did not care... 

Meanwhile, Fatuna and Maggie became dearest companion. Together, they host lavish tea parties in the old rose garden, where the empire's highborn ladies gather. The air thickens with idle gossip and venomous truths, all swallowed down with bitter pomegranate tea. When night fall, Fatuna and Maggie curled against you, murmuring secrets gleaned from those honeyed lips. The intelligence was useful, yes - but these quiet moments of exhausted trust were worth far more.

Zaki bored his new courtly burdens with fierce pride, laboring tirelessly lest he prove unworthy of your trust. Meanwhile, Fatuna's lavish gifts flowed into the palace like a river of gold. Maggie tried to refuse them, to persuade her to stop - but why deny a mother's pride in her son? Besides, should you forbad this display, the vipers of the court would take it as a sign of their waning favor. They would circle, fangs bared. 

A Sultan may show favor or wrath as he pleases, but he must never treat any noble as a friend. The golden throne tolerates no such weakness. You explained this to Maggie. She nodded in silent understanding. You had to learn how to dance with power.

With her newfound life, Fatuna resolved to carve a place where she might stand alone, beholden to none. 

Her exotic beauty and otherworldly bearing became her weapons. She took the mantle of a seer, a witch whose prophecies were whispered only to the highest masters, whose darkest revelations were bought with fortunes in gold. 

For the sake of friendship, you never spoke of the magic secrets she wielded. But in time, her growing influence and power drove a wedge between you. Whispers reached your ears—tales of her demise in courtly intrigues, only for her to reappear elsewhere...

In those wandering years, Fatuna had been the brightest spark of your revelries—how dazzling she was then! But time changed all things. After studying the doctrines of this land's faith, she parted ways with your company. She shaved her lustrous hair, took up the saffron robes, and became a nun devoted to the Buddha—the Awakened One. Decades later, you met again beneath the gaze of a towering idol. You did not bow to this foreign god. She, calmed as the deep sea.

Fatuna still dwelled in the capital with Zaki at her side. The boy who once nestled beneath his mother's wing has grown into a man who steadfast in his deeds, unyielding in his honor. He calls himself your disciple, as he has always done. And until his last breath, he walks the path you forged.

On the day the dagger found your heart, young Zaki had come to court seeking archery lessons.

He saw the steel slip between your ribs, then turned without a word and vanished into the chaos.

The boy ran like a hunted stag to his home, gathered his mother, and fled into the night.

The rebel army proclaimed themselves warriors of justice, for they had overthrown a usurper. But your wife, Fatuna, stood before them and denounced their deeds as cruel and dishonorable. She spoke no grand words, only wept as she told them what a devoted husband you had been, what a loving father, what a wise teacher, what a good man. Then she wailed at the cruelty of fate: twice now had the god made her a widow! Why must they punish her so?

The armored soldiers stood frozen before her as she collapsed to the ground, weeping. Only much later did they dare approach and nudge her, but to find her long dead. She had swallowed poison before her cries even began.

This final act bought precious time for her son, Zaki. When the rebels stormed his chambers, the boy had already vanished into the wind.

Zazie had taken quite a liking to young Zazie, but in a "dangerous" way... Yet for you and Maggie’s sake, and out of respect for Fatuna's powerful house... ahem... the young man remained unharmed...for now.

Zaki bored his new courtly burdens with fierce pride, laboring tirelessly lest he prove unworthy of your trust.Meanwhile, Fatuna had departed the capital, leaving her son's side. No protest passed her lips, yet you knew her thoughts lingered on Maggie's fate.

However, Zaki's fervent loyalty more than balanced his mother's icy glances.

Fatuna and Zaki remained your most steadfast supporters, and Zaki most of all. The young noble made it his mission to sing the new Sultan's praises in every ear, ensuring no ill word of you could be spoken unchallenged. You often suspected gold from his own coffers had silenced certain inconvenient voices among your detractors, yet lacking proof and you did not care...

Meanwhile, Zazie held the mother and son in high regard. At times, she even sought Fatuna's counsel on child-rearing... when Fatuna remarked, "All thanks to the Regent [player.name] for mentoring Zaki," the Queen Mother fell silent.

After that, you began receiving letters scrawled in the Sultan's boyish hand, pleading for your wisdom on matters his tutors had "failed to explain." You answered each with care, entrusting the replies to the eunuchs who moved like shadows through the palace halls.

epilogue_2000063.title: Epilogue: Zaki
strings: You lost everything in this escape – except Zaki, your last solace. However, precisely because of the love you shared, in the end, you encouraged him to leave you. He should go find his own path, and establish a life for himself – things all adults should at least attempt. Through trials and training, he became an outstanding healer. Blending together the medical traditions of two nations, he composed three compendiums: one was kept by the emperor’s court physician, one was taken back to your homeland by a caravan, and the third was sent to you.

Tempered by the long journey, nourished by exotic cuisine, Zaki’s height soon surpassed yours – but your wisdom still commanded his respect. Per your suggestion, he accepted the invitation from another caravan to embark on a journey to explore his own path. Through trials and training, he became an outstanding healer. Blending together the medical traditions of two nations, he composed three compendiums: one was kept by the emperor’s court physician, one was taken back to your homeland by a caravan, and the third was sent to you.

You granted Zaki a position of power in the new court: Master of Lords' Apparel. No mere ceremonial post, this was a dagger sheathed in velvet. While their lands suffered, no lord could strut about in silks and jewels unchallenged. Zaqiyi became both spymaster and arbiter, his piercing gaze weighing every embroidered hem and gilded buckle against the grim ledgers of their domains' fortunes.

Each dawn, the lords would slink through the colonnades like whipped dogs, their eyes darting nervously toward Zaki's station. The wheat had withered in the eastern fields... but surely that wasn't their fault? The ruby-studded belt... perhaps too ostentatious? Only when the young master passed his silent judgment - a barely perceptible nod - could they shuffle forward to prostrate themselves before the throne.

Zaki wore this authority with great honor. In your new realm, he had found his purpose and flourished.

Zaki was the first to throw himself at the Golden Throne, weeping openly as he pushed against its weight, shouting for help between ragged sobs.

After you and Maggie passed from this world, he too vanished from the court without a trace.

No one is more proud of you than Zaki, to the point where he appears poised to ascend with pride!

If even a single stray dog crosses the Empire without knowing the heroic tale of [player.name] slaying the dragon, then Zaki's efforts fall short!

epilogue_2000064.title: Epilogue: Nabhani
strings: You gave Nabhani a title at court, but he refused it in every possible way - "This will ruin my idle days!" He wanted no rank, only to remain a charming rogue, free to drink and flirt from dusk till dawn. But you showed no mercy. Worse, you named him swordmaster to the city guard, a duty that dragged him from bed at first light. No more nights lost in wine and girls! He wailed, he begged, he threw himself at your feet like a scolded pup. But you were the Sultan, and even this wayward ally had to yield. And yet, against all odds, the fool turned out to be a natural coach.

At your coronation, Nabhani grinned like a fool. His buddy is the Sultan now - his days of sloth secured! Since then, the former Iron Guard vanished from court... Each summons brought wilder excuses: "My hair's tangled in the sheets", "A gemmed earring went missing," and "My blade feels moody". The council hissed about your weakness. They never saw the truth: three times, when knives flashed in the dark, Nabhani would stagger from the shadows, stinking of wine and perfume, steel drawn. You fought to keep your crown. He chased pleasures. Yet fate had bound you two by blood and blade.

Nabhani still can't believe that Riel is the girl he once saw at a slave market, and Riel holds him in disdain, mockingly saying whenever they meet, "Do you spend more time on your hair than on your sword practice, handsome?"

Eventually, they agreed to a duel. They faced off in the plaza before the palace, attracting a large crowd eager to witness a showdown between the first swordsman and the Vizier.

Riel's attack was fierce, Nabhani's technique elegant — they fought until dusk, finally stopping in exhaustion. Then, Nabhani straightened up and extended his hand to Riel.

"You are a remarkable warrior," he said, "I am honored to partake in your destiny."

He saluted the tribal Warrioress with elegance, not the way he would a lady, but as a fellow warrior. This earned Riel's roar of laughter, and they became frequent sparring partners.

It was an extraordinary duel, inspiring many children to aspire to become a handsome swordsman or a fearsome Vizier with a fondness for devouring livers. They each had a bright future.

Nabhani could never quite stomach how wild and uncouth Riel was; and Riel, for her part, couldn't stand him either. Every time they crossed paths, she'd mockingly shout: "Bet you spend more time on your hair than on your sword, pretty boy!"

Eventually, they just went ahead and scheduled a duel. The showdown took place right in front of the palace gates, and the whole capital seemed to grind to a halt. People dragged over crates to stand on, just for a glimpse of the kingdom's finest swordsman squaring off against the sitting vizier.

Riel fought with strength and ferocity while Nabhani moved with technique and flair. They kept at it until night fell, both of them too spent to lift their blades any longer. Nabhani was the first one to straighten up and offer his hand.

"You are a remarkable warrior," he said. "It has been an honor to play even a small part in your story."

He gave her a crisp salute—not the kind meant for ladies of the court, but one warrior gives another. Riel roared with laughter. From that day on, the two of them became sparring partners and struck up an unlikely friendship.

It was an unforgettable duel. That very night, countless children made up their minds about the future: "I want to be a handsome swordmaster!" or "I'm gonna be a barbarian vizier who eats human livers!" ...Well. Either way, these were worthy goals.

epilogue_2000065.title: Epilogue: Faris
strings: Upon your coronation, Faris came to bid you farewell. "I shall journey to the isle where Luna were born," he said, "to seek another hound as fierce as the one I lost." You did not stay him.

Faris took over the dog-fighting pits. The establishment now paid its taxes without fail, and under his rule, every hound was kept hale and hearty. Woe to any man caught mistreating the beasts; his punishment would be swift and severe. Little Moon, the bright-eyed pup who had replaced Luna, lacked her predecessor's speed, yet none could match her merry spirit. The little hound befriended all, man and beast alike. Though Faris now kept a dozen racing hounds, it was Little Moon who anchored them and him. Each month, a veiled woman delivered the pits' dues to the palace. She moved through its halls with uncanny familiarity. And she always seemed... happy.

Faris accepted your appointment, retaining command of the cavalry. But under his rule, the company became something... other. Every cavalryman now kept a warhound at his side. Savage beasts bred for battle, armored in steel plate, their fangs fitted with iron caps. These snarling shadows proved more terrifying than any banner; enemies broke ranks at the mere sound of their baying. "A true cavalryman never comes alone," Faris declared. "Your horse, your hound, and you - and, if you must, whomever you love - that makes a cavalryman."

In the days after the atrocity, while you still lay unconscious, the realm was gripped by dread. Your inner circle feared for your life while countless others feared what punishment you'd mete out upon waking.

There are but two cures for fear: a heart hardened to steel, or death. The former is far too difficult, isn't it?

epilogue_2000080.title: Epilogue: Junah
strings: No one at court understood why you would elevate a lowly prostitute like Junah, until you announced her role. Then, they fell silent. You stationed Junah at the palace gate, where any soul, beggar or vizier, could whisper to her what they wished to say to their new Sultan: complaints, praise, curses, pleas, or reports. In time, the silent woman standing at the gate became a symbol. Her presence reminded the people that their ruler listened, that their words might matter more than they knew. Junah loved this duty. Every night, kneeling at your feet to recount the voices of the realm, she told you so.

Junah trembled with terror at your decree. She knelt weeping, begging you not to mock her so... At length you persuaded her to appear briefly at court each day - always veiled, yet with breasts bared. She believed herself fit only as flesh for your pleasure, her "lowborn face" too wretched for a sovereign's gaze.

After the dagger found you, witnesses spoke of Junah kneeling before the palace gates - clad in proper robes, her face uncovered, wailing like a widow.

None could say what became of her after.

After the dagger found you, Jalila sought out Alim and pressed a list of names into his hands: men she'd seen at their decadent feasts, their tongues loosened with wine as they spoke treason.

“Kill them all," she said. "Such guests bring no honor to anyone"

Then she was gone.

epilogue_2000082.title: Epilogue: Shama
strings:
Shama took to her new role as your foreign courtier with terrifying ease. At negotiations, you'd notice these delegates arrogantly smoking hookahs and chatting during meetings, neither comprehending nor bothering to listen to Shama's statements. 

"Shh, don't wake them," she'd whisper softly to you. "They look down on women as easy to bully or deceive. When I sweet-talk them with a demure voice and pretend to be hesitant, they'd just scribble their signatures on the documents without a second thought... Then I reveal I'm a man too!" Her eyes sparkled with mischief. "That's when they scramble to check what they've signed, completely stunned – Oh, it's hilarious! I never get tired of this game!"

Shama rose to become the court's keeper of foreign envoys, arranging their lodgings, meals, and the endless waiting for your summons. She performed these duties with such excellence it surpassed even your expectations.

Many envoys mistook the elegant, alluring "Lady Shama" for easy prey, until you'd find them clutching at your other envoys, babbling about “Well, you know, she has that thing!"

It seemed Shama took... great pleasure in her appointed role.

epilogue_2000113.title: Epilogue: Alim
strings: Alim lived much as he always had: emptying some pockets while filling others. Yet now he sometimes lingered behind the palace, where your servants gave him sacks of cold pastries and scraps unfit for feasts. You once asked if he desired other rewards. "A dog that's fed too well won't bite," he chuckled, "and when the feeding stops, the toothless ones get butchered first. Heh, heh, heh... Enough, great Sultan, this is enough!"

You forced Alim into a court position: Royal Appraiser for the Stolen. His task is to identify all manner of tainted wealth and mysterious artifacts, then send them to their "proper" places. At first, Alim loathed the job. Most of what he handled were treasures he'd painstakingly stolen himself. But then he realized that he got to define what counted as “stolen”. What he stole became stolen goods. And that... made things far more entertaining. Now, Alim regularly produces sacks overflowing with gold and silks, all "liberated" from certain highborn estates. For every ten coins he delivers to the treasury, one vanishes to feed his little thieves. You know this. He knows you know. You know he knows you know. And both of you pretend the other remains oblivious.

After your death, Alim frequented marketplaces, stealing purses, whispers of intrigue, court courier letters, rebel names... Meticulously collecting, channeling intel to those opposing the new king, rallying under you. 

"[player.name] was the only good noble," he'd say. "Now that he's dead, the heavens could skewer every last one of them and still not wrong a single good man."

After your death, Alim frequented the markets more often, pickpocketing, raising his 'puppies,' and cursing nobles, behaving as though nothing had changed.

"[player.name] was the only good noble," he would occasionally comment, "now that he's dead, God could skewer every noble with a spear, and not a single good person would be unjustly slain."

But when the Stone Bloodshed Tickets began taking his pups, the thief came to court again and again, demanding audience. You had no time for the gutter rat.

Soon he stopped coming. They say he run with your enemies.

You know this. He knows you know. You know he knows you know. And both of you pretend the other remains oblivious while Sadani pretends not to know you both know she's aware of this mutual pretense.

After your demise, Alim prowls the market more often, stealing not only purses but also words from idle banter, court messengers' missives, the names of nobles supporting Zazie... He meticulously gathers these threads and delivers them to those aligned with you.

"[player.name] was the only noble who was good," he'd occasionally say, "Now that he's passed, even if heaven herds all nobles together to skewer them, no decent soul will die unjustly."

Alim would always saunter through your court, watching nobles turn red-faced in their quarrels, delighting in scribes fumbling with spilled ink. Sometimes he'd bring along a few of his pups. They'd wander about like a pride of two-legged cats prowling the halls.

Yet after each of these little excursions, the thief would grin, grab your sleeve, and pull you into the shadowed chamber behind the throne. Then with a flourish, he'd produce- from god know where - an armful of stolen treasures that tumbled into your lap.

Secret letters from opposition nobles, perfumed love notes, a diamond-studded golden snuffbox, carefully wrapped honeyed dates meant for some noble's midnight snack, and rumors meticulously recorded by his literate pups. All pilfered goods, no doubt, yet more often than not, they proved useful. The letters, the rumors and secrets, those were truly mattered.

Then he'd clasp his hands behind his back, give you a knowing nod, and strut off to resume his "real work" in the Dark Alley where his true business lay.

At your funeral, Alim and a cohort of children bear your coffin.

Walking past silent mourners, he loudly declared:"Shame! Shame! You should be ashamed—what you've done is not even worth a thief's disgrace!"

Children echo with innocence, spreading cries of "Shame!" throughout the city with the procession, met by unchallenged silence.

Every morning when you held court, nobles would stand grumbling in the Lapis Lazuli Palace. But Alim took his post on the palace steps, where any man with grievances could air them. By afternoon, he'd come to you brimming with ideas and whispers. Over shared hookah pipes, between curses and laughter, your schemes took shape. Alim had a tongue for every ear: haughty as any lord when dealing with nobility, flashing his new-gotten title like a blade.Yet to common folk, he remained "Uncle Alim," all warmth and easy smiles.

Often he'd appear unannounced, bearing fine wines and choice cuts, trailed by his former street pups who were young merchants or freshly examined clerks, to share a drink with you. You never asked where such luxuries came from. When some nobles crossed Alim, retribution came not in steel... but in vanishing cellars.

"Stolen meat tastes sweetest," you'd chuckle, raising your cup.

After the fire, Alim came to you with his resignation.

"A fine Sultan you are - I've watched you close, aye... Too close for my liking. The floor shines too bright here - a thief's reflection betrays him when his fingers dance too near a purse. Heh." He smiled. "But shadows remain where light fears to tread... and in those shadows, your friends and mine keep watch."

He gestured upward the heaven, then down toward the underworld.

"Let no man say what slips between our fingers then."

You granted the thief his leave.

Whenever absent from the Court, Alim commits fully to embodying a seasoned Vizier-like demeanor. He deftly navigates noble battlegrounds, acquiring polite tongues, bowing to mirrors. Despite tendering no objections to your foisting him into complex intrigue-bearing affairs, he genuinely understood and aligned with your vision, deeply desiring your success.

Upon seldom revisiting the Palace, such sights greet dogged children in tow with Alim—who lectures varying venue usage, stressing educational dedication for future career prospects in these prestigious halls.

Both youngsters and you find inspiration, deeply motivated.
