epilogue_2000123.title: Epilogue: Lumera
strings: As Lumera ventured beyond the empire's borders, her vision widened. She had read thousands of books, walked thousands of miles, and met innumerable souls. In time, her wisdom and magic grew beyond mortal bounds, and in the mouths of the locals, she became an immortal of legends. In the end, such fame has became a burden. They made her decision inevitable: to leave the mortal realm behind. It is said that when she ascended Kunlun, five immortals descended from the heavens to welcome you. But in the howling blizzard, all you saw was her smile, as she turned to look at you for the final time.

During your sailings, Lumera awoke to the voice of the wind. The way she bent the weather and tides to her will made her a legend among sailors of the Seven Seas. In time, she forged a supernatural bond with a pod of whales, and in the end, left your fleet to join them. But whenever the storms raged and the waves towered high, her and her friends would appear to guide your flagship to safety.

The supreme emperor once sought to make Lumera his bride. But after conversing with her at length, he granted her a holier purpose – to extend his life and forge the fabled elixir of immortality. The great altar and the sky-gold furnace drained the empire's coffers dry. But you knew the truth – this was no path to eternal life. 

At last, before the Emperor's very eyes, Lumera jumped into the furnace. She was remade, transfigured by sacred rites, shedding the dust of mortality and ascending at last to the fate she had long been denied: A star, burning high above, watching over the world below. 

This was no path meant for mortal men. As this dynasty drew to its end, three emperors perished after swallowing the ashes from the sky-gold furnace. The last, in a final act of desperation, threw himself into the flames, chasing the elusive possibility of apotheosis. The chronicles all put the blame you, the treacherous courtier of foreign blood. But by then, you were of course long gone.

Lumera walked the breadth of this land with you. You saw its rivers and valleys, its peaks and forests. Until, at last, on a mist-wreathed cliffside, she found her fate. All you remember is the rain, the shimmering fog, and the laughter of goddesses, ringing like chimes in a dream. And she was gone.

Fardak's tribe kept close ties with your new empire. You granted his father the title of ruler of a vassal state. In gratitude, Fardak came to pay homage with his wife. They seemed happy. Lumera smiled more now, and Fardak never missed a single one of those smiles. When they left, they... “ransacked” half your royal library. Well, never mind.

Fardak's tribe kept close ties with your new empire. You granted his father the title of ruler of a vassal state. In gratitude, Fardak came to pay homage with his wife. Four days after their departure, a coup occurred in which you were slain. Never again did Fardak's people treat with the Sultan's empire. Every ruler who followed, whether with steel or silk, demanded their fealty. But their answer remained: "My wife and I have pledged to one great Sultan. We shall have no other."

Fardak's tribe kept close ties with your New Sun empire. You granted his father the title of ruler of a vassal state. In gratitude, Fardak came to pay homage with his wife. Lumera smiled more now, and Fardak never missed a single one of those smiles. 

Before departing, they lingered long in your chambers. You spoke of the burdens of rule, warning Fardak to walk carefully between tradition and change. He nodded thoughtfully, though perhaps not fully grasping your meaning, while his wife watched you with wide, silent eyes. You could only hope they heard you true.
Lumera has lost your shelter, but do not worry about her. She became the most learned sage of her age, every true account of your reign, every impartial record of your deeds, flowed from her quill.

Fardak's tribe kept close ties with your New Sun empire. You granted his father the title of ruler of a vassal state. In gratitude, Fardak came to pay homage with his wife.

After the dagger found your heart, his people alone kept their oaths. When your successor marched to break this defiance, a queer darkness fell upon the battlefield as they breached the clan's gates. Then came the sky-fire where great burning stones hurled from the heavens, scattering imperial warriors like broken toys.

None dared trouble the Star-Souled clan again.

Fardak's tribe kept close ties with your New Sun empire. You granted his father the title of ruler of a vassal state. In gratitude, Fardak came to pay homage with his wife.

Lumera smiled more now, and Fardak never missed a single one of those smiles.

Before departing, they lingered long in your chambers. You spoke of the burdens of rule, warning Fardak to walk carefully between tradition and change. He nodded thoughtfully, though perhaps not fully grasping your meaning, while his wife watched you with wide, silent eyes.

You could only hope they heard you true.

Fardak and Lumera sat bewildered at your feet before departing the capital, their voices thick with disbelief. "Why?" they pressed, "Why this? Did you not despise the game most bitterly? Was it not you who stood against the last Sultan's game? And now you would make this realm... a Realm of Game?"

You merely smiled. "When I counseled against it, I had not yet learned to play."

They exchanged silent glances, then bowed in farewell.

You never saw their faces again.

Fardak's tribe kept close ties with your empire. You granted his father the title of ruler of a vassal state. In gratitude, Fardak came to pay homage with his wife.

They seemed happy. Lumera smiled more now, and Fardak never missed a single one of those smiles.

When they left, they... “ransacked” half your royal library. Well, never mind.

Fardak's tribe kept close ties with your new empire. As the Regent, you granted his father the title of ruler of a vassal state. In gratitude, Fardak came to pay homage with his wife. Four days after their departure, a coup occurred in which you were slain.

Never again did Fardak's people treat with the Sultan's empire. Every ruler who followed, whether with steel or silk, demanded their fealty. But their answer remained:

"My wife and I have pledged to one great master. We shall have no other."

Over a year later, a book named "Under Lamplight" began spreading through the alleys and taverns. A story of a ruler who bled for his people, only to meet his end by their very hands. None with wits doubted whose shadow lay beneath those words.

The book was... more than well-written. Its prose flowed like blackberry wine, its twists sharper than a steel blade. But what truly cut was its sorrow that few who turned its pages left with dry eyes. And with each tear, your ghost grew. No longer just a rebel's banner, but an idea, a way of thinking and a sigil carved into people's hearts.

The author's name? Lumera.

When the dust settled, a council of your followers seized the reins of power. They kept your reforms alive and declared the day of your murder a day of mourning.

Through countless trials and betrayals, through years the histories would forget... your vision took root. The realm would remember your name, your dream of every individual born equal, of chains broken.

The chronicler who recorded these truths and bound them in leather was a woman called Lumera, and her work titled "The Guilty Stone". When the last page was inked, she vanished from all records. In that same season, stargazers swore a new light burned in the empire's heavens, a star unseen before.

Lumera was named Keeper of the Royal Library.

No appointment could have suited her better. Just ask for any tome, name any author, and she'd point unerringly to its shelf and niche, reciting its contents.

Years into her service, a curious thing appeared among the stacks: a delicate brass-and-gilt shelf, your gift to her. There, gleaming softly in the lamplight, stood every book she'd ever penned.

epilogue_2000199.title: Epilogue: Asal
strings: You began handing your manuscripts to The Angler’s owner, merely to exchange words with a man of letters. But when your writings gained immense popularity, the letters started coming with endless, ink-stained demands for more. Ugh, that was annoying. By the way, he specifically established a bookstore branch, and named it “Double-Headed Dragon”.

epilogue_2000312.title: Epilogue: Nawfal
strings: Nawfal chose to withdraw from court as well, settling within easy reach of your estate. On occasion, you'd cross paths in the only proper bookstore this side of the city. The smell of parchment and ink would take you back—to The Angler, to those Sultan Cards, to the brutal games you once played... At least that's done with. You glanced up. Your old rival exhaled sharply through his nose, as if sharing the very thought.

Nawfal remained in the new regime, partly by your request, but mostly because he'd found a purpose brighter than burning down the old world. Slowly, methodically, with that quiet ruthlessness of his, he expanded your Nursery. 

Street urchins became scholars; scholars became clerks, tutors, stewards. And each child carried the same lesson: Your success buys the next one's chance. They worked like starving hounds chasing a scent. His letters arrive often now, ink smudged with immense happiness, addressing you as "My most stubborn enemy" and "My only true friend in this lifetime".

Nawfal remained in the court. The throne had new faces, but power forever steeped in venom, like gold always mixed with base copper in the mines. So he stayed, weary and short-tempered, the weight of it all pressing upon him... until the day he could bear no more. Then his ravens would come, bearing furious words meant for your eyes alone. After all, you were his most stubborn rival, the only man who'd ever matched him blow for blow and the closest thing to a friend he had left in this world.

Nawfal remained in the new regime, partly by your request, but mostly because he'd found a purpose brighter than burning down the old world. Slowly, methodically, with that quiet ruthlessness of his, he expanded your Nursery. Street urchins became scholars; scholars became clerks, tutors, stewards. And each child carried the same lesson: Your success buys the next one's chance. They worked like starving hounds chasing a scent. His letters arrive often now, ink smudged with immense happiness, addressing you as "My most stubborn enemy" and "My only true friend in this lifetime".

At first, Nawfal refused the Vizier's seat several times.. "A man who wants to be the Sultan should never wear the crown," you told him. "And those who grovel for the title of Vizier'? They're the last men you'd trust with power." 

He nearly yielded, but in the end, he insisted on a trial by words. A hundred souls stood before the court, each given five minutes to prove their worth. You sat beside Nawfal, weighing their speeches, judging if they could be next Vizier'. But none close. None better than Nawfal. And so, for years after, he served as your sharpest Vizier' and the most relentless adviser, like a pale gadfly hovering around you.

When you took power, the former Sultan's favorites vanished. His sycophants, his fools, his loyal dogs, all fled the city like whipped curs. You let them go. Gave them two days, even. A ruler has no use for men who flee, and dead weight only clutters a capital. 

But Nawfal remained. 

He clung to your court like a burr to wool, scribbling those endless, venomous tracts. Once your policies grow unjust, when your edicts steal the people's peace, there his words would be, sharp as a gadfly's bite...

For seventy-seven days, Nawfal ruled as the perfect Vizier. Then the knives found you, and the traitors dragged him to the pyre, demanding he denounce you as a tyrannical, incompetent ruler. 

"My Sultan had but one flaw," he sneered at them," that he made me his Vizier, a weak, witless fool who failed to purge vermin like you. This fire is no less than I deserve." 

Even as the flames engulfed him, his final breaths echoed with shouts of your name. To this day, men still say "loyal as Nawfal" when they speak of true service.

When you took power, Nawfal vanished from the capital. And when you were overthrown and assassinated, he did not raise his voice in your defense. People whispered that he must have hated you still, that he reveled in your fall. But in secret, he rescued all those who had benefited from you and survived from new Sultan's purge. In his hermitage, he established a school for the poorest children where the survivors became teachers. 

Years later, usurper's name faded into obscurity. But the tales of you, [player.name], and that brief dawn when the New Sun illuminated the empire, spread across the land through the lips of the graduates.

When the treachery that doomed you unfolded, your warriors fought with their lives on the line. Some nearly died dragging you from the ambush. Others led desperate cavalry charges to hold back the tide. More still barricaded the palace gates with their own bodies, choosing to perish alongside their foes over surrender. Yet one man prevented their sacrifice. Not out of cowardice, not from lack of devotion. 

"To die here is wasteful," Nawfal told your bleeding champions, "We serve only one Sultan, [player.name]. If he is gone, then this land shall have no other. We have overthrown Sultan before. We can do so again." 

Thus did Nawfal gather your surviving Iron Guards - Nabhani, Seliman, Jabal, and Faris, carving from your former lands a rebel state. Within months, they raised new armies, seized supplies, and struck at the usurper's forces. Where they marched, people who remembered your rule flocked to their banners. For years they waged their war, your likeness stitched upon every standard. When at last they stormed the Lapis Lazuli Palace, every survivor bore the scars of that long struggle. Your Iron Guards donned their old vestments once more. Loyalists filled the court again. Nawfal leaned against a pillar, idly turning pages of that book you'd gifted him long ago. For a fleeting moment, time seemed to unwind, as if you might stride through those doors at any instant... Then Nawfal placed your crown upon the vacant throne in people's sobs. He proclaimed the new order: He would rule as the Vizier, with the Sultan's seat empty for now. In later generations, this peculiar reign was remembered as "The Empty Throne."

Nawfal accepted the title of Vizier in silence. He knew, just as you knew, the title demanded he bare his teeth against the realm's circling jackals, ever watchful for daggers in the dark, for poisoned whispers, for the slow erosion of his name. He even declined your rewards to uphold his political principles: "A crown's grace should not reward those already gorged on power." 

For a fleeting time, the two of you almost believed change was possible. His pale hands steadied the scepter you could barely lift. But two months later, Nawfal was assassinated. The killers made little effort to hide their triumph. They celebrated death of the "Gadfly", that incorruptible, honestest man. With him gone, your rule bled from its first wound. You raged, dozens of heads rolled and five houses were stripped of name and privilege. 

The nobles called you tyrant, but you'd make the same choice again with no regret. Had Nawfal lived, he would likely do the same.

Nawfal was not your new Vizier, and he was content with this arrangement. He served the realm while stepping back from the game of thrones... Yet he understood your precarious position all too well: how every step forward was met by twice as many hands dragging you back. So he chose to aid you differently, from the shadows. 

He expanded the Nursery you had created together, establishing new branches in every major city. No longer just for the poorest children, these Nurseries now welcomed commoners' sons, bankrupt nobles' offspring, even slaves' children. 

Nawfal summoned those who had survived the Sultan's games with you to teach there, pouring every ounce of his will into planting seeds of justice, fairness, and wisdom in those young minds. He placed his hopes in the next generation or the one after that. In a future neither of you would live to see. 

The nobles scoffed at Nawfal's class-dissolving ideas as perilous absurdity - slaves learning beside nobles? You shuffled, demurred, changed the subject each time the issue arose... It was all you could do. You two never wrote. Never spoke. Yet the trust between you remained unbroken.

Nawfal was not your new Vizier, and he was content with this arrangement. He served the realm while stepping back from the game of thrones... Yet he pitied you deeply. You were trapped in a gilded cage, and worse, you had walked into it willingly. 

Away from court, Nawfal kept his quill sharp. From time to time, he published scathing commentaries on the realm's ills. Once, he had railed against the Sultan; now, he still railed against the Sultan - that is to say, you. Every criticism struck true, yet you could do nothing. Your hands were bound, the ropes cutting bloody grooves into your very soul. 

Strangely, reading his words brought you an odd lightness. For in those moments, you remembered your fierce debates in the Sultan's court, how Naefil's rebut had never dulled. He remained sharp as ever, still believing in justice, still fighting for a better realm. He was still himself. And that, at least, was something unchanging in this world. 

You never saw each other again.

Nawfal accepted your appointment reluctantly, becoming your Vasir. Throughout your shared year of governance, he remarked not less than five hundred times, 'If only you were a tad more patient, we might devise better explanations...' As he continued dissecting layered, intricate affairs, he served excellently. 

He died like a noble Vasir: following your assassination, Nawfal ingested poison in his study, leaving no farewell.

After your coronation, Nawfal shed his opposition like an old cloak and became your most vocal defender. His new foes were the courtiers who still whispered "usurper" behind their sleeves. For hours they would duel with words in the throne room, debating legitimacy, tradition, whether a ruler's worth was measured in peace and prosperity, whether overthrowing tyranny could ever truly be called treason...

The endless quarrels drained him. His face grew gaunt, his hands unsteady, until at last you commanded him to retire to his lands for two months' rest. And on the eve of his intended return, the dagger found you.

Nawfal never came back to the capital again. He raised his levies, sealed his borders, and let his domain become a sovereign splinter in the realm's flesh. The Sultans who followed were as short-lived as the last, and could spare no swords for some backwater fief. Years turned, and from that isolated county emerged young men and women with sharp minds and tongues, all raised to know one truth: that [player.name] was the Sultan who forged greatness, never the shameless usurper.

Nawfal accepted the title of Vizier in silence. He knew, just as you knew, the title demanded he bare his teeth against the realm's circling jackals, ever watchful for daggers in the dark, for poisoned whispers, for the slow erosion of his name. He even declined your rewards to uphold his political principles: "A crown's grace should not reward those already gorged on power."

For a fleeting time, the two of you almost believed change was possible. His pale hands steadied the scepter you could barely lift.

But two months later, Nawfal was assassinated.

The killers made little effort to hide their triumph. They celebrated death of the "Gadfly", that incorruptible, honestest man.

With him gone, your rule bled from its first wound. You raged, dozens of heads rolled and five houses were stripped of name and privilege.

The nobles called you tyrant, but you'd make the same choice again with no regret.

Had Nawfal lived, he would likely do the same.

Nawfal was not your new Vizier, and he was content with this arrangement. He served the realm while stepping back from the game of thrones... Yet he understood your precarious position all too well: how every step forward was met by twice as many hands dragging you back. So he chose to aid you differently, from the shadows.

He expanded the Nursery you had created together, establishing new branches in every major city. No longer just for the poorest children, these Nurseries now welcomed commoners' sons, bankrupt nobles' offspring, even slaves' children. Nawfal summoned those who had survived the Sultan's games with you to teach there, pouring every ounce of his will into planting seeds of justice, fairness, and wisdom in those young minds. He placed his hopes in the next generation or the one after that. In a future neither of you would live to see.

The nobles scoffed at Nawfal's class-dissolving ideas as perilous absurdity - slaves learning beside nobles? You shuffled, demurred, changed the subject each time the issue arose... It was all you could do.

You two never wrote. Never spoke. Yet the trust between you remained unbroken.

Nawfal was not your new Vizier, and he was content with this arrangement. He served the realm while stepping back from the game of thrones... Yet he pitied you deeply. You were trapped in a gilded cage, and worse, you had walked into it willingly.

Away from court, Nawfal kept his quill sharp. From time to time, he published scathing commentaries on the realm's ills. Once, he had railed against the Sultan; now, he still railed against the Sultan - that is to say, you. Every criticism struck true, yet you could do nothing. Your hands were bound, the ropes cutting bloody grooves into your very soul.

Strangely, reading his words brought you an odd lightness. For in those moments, you remembered your fierce debates in the Sultan's court, how Naefil's rebut had never dulled. He remained sharp as ever, still believing in justice, still fighting for a better realm. He was still himself. And that, at least, was something unchanging in this world.

You never saw each other again.

Nawfal retreated to his lands with a band of your dissenters, where they stubbornly rejected the Joyous Tickets, hanging every courier who dared deliver them outside their walls. They raised armies, barred their gates, with a pitiful show of defiance.

You relished their slow torment. After all, did this rebellious city not deserve the honor of a Gold Conquest? The only question remained: to whose hands should you entrust this glorious task...

At first, Nawfal refused the Vizier's seat several times.. "A man who wants to be the Sultan should never wear the crown," you told him. "And those who grovel for the title of Vizier? They're the last men you'd trust with power."

He nearly yielded, but in the end, he insisted on a trial by words. A hundred souls stood before the court, each given five minutes to prove their worth. You sat beside Nawfal, weighing their speeches, judging if they could be next Vizier.

But none close. None better than Nawfal. And so, for years after, he served as your sharpest Vizier and the most relentless adviser, like a pale gadfly hovering around you.

When you took power, the former Sultan's favorites vanished. His sycophants, his fools, his loyal dogs, all fled the city like whipped curs. You let them go. Gave them two days, even. A ruler has no use for men who flee, and dead weight only clutters a capital.

But Nawfal remained. He clung to your court like a burr to wool, scribbling those endless, venomous tracts. Once your policies grow unjust, when your edicts steal the people's peace, there his words would be, sharp as a gadfly's bite...

Nawfal stood among the nobles gathered before the throne to witness Sadani and her son ascend to power. Many nobles stole glances at him: had he raised his voice in protest, they would have roared with him.

Yet Nawfal remained silent. He bowed deeply to the new Sultan, the boy's mother, and the Regent without a word of dissent. In time, you named him Vizier, and together you labored to untangle the knotted mess of succession...When the realm at last knew a fragile peace, Nawfal came to you with books and fine wine.

"I feared," he confessed, "what if you failed to carve out even a shred of legitimacy? What if, to survive and to claim the throne.. you became the very thing we fought against?"

You asked what he thought of the new Sultan.

"The boy?" He laughed, shaking his head. "At least he has a worthy Regent."

You drank until the hour grew late.

After your death, Sadani came to Nawfal, urging him to remain as Vizier and pledge his loyalty to the realm.

With him at the court, she argued, there might yet be hope to preserve stability. She offered him riches, titles, even the Regency itself.

"You are mistaken, concubine Sadani," Nawfal replied, his gaze heavy with sorrow. "A man who desires to be Regent is the last man fit to rule. Those who hunger for power will always abuse it, that is why we must place it only in the hands of those who fear it. [Player.Name] understood this. You do not."

With reverence, he knelt before the little Sultan and begged leave to resign. He had lost a dear friend, he said, and grief had left him unfit to serve. To execute him would only spark rebellion, so Sadani granted his request.

Nawfal returned to his land, where he raised high walls and mustered armies, shielding his domain from the crumbling empire. In the decades and centuries that followed, his territory bred many great souls, all weaned on a little book penned by Nawfal himself: "My Adversary, [Player.Name]."

When you took power, Nawfal vanished from the capital.

And when you were assassinated, he did not raise his voice in your defense. People whispered that he must have hated you still, that he reveled in your fall. But in secret, he rescued all those who had benefited from you and survived from Queen Mother's purge. In his hermitage, he established a school for the poorest children where the survivors became teachers.

Years later, when the little Sultan lay dead and warlords painted the realm in blood, when a hundred petty realms rose and fell unremembered - it was the graduates of this humble school who carried your tale across the continent. Of how you overthrew the tyrant. How you played the Sultan's game... and chose justice.

When word of Realm of Game's plan reached Nawfal, he came to the palace seeking audience with you. You denied him.

For three days and three nights he kept vigil at your gates. Then he left.

From that day until long after, the realm knew no Vizier again.

When the dagger found you, and the traitors dragged Nawfal to the pyre, demanding he denounce you as a tyrannical, incompetent ruler.

"My Sultan had but one flaw," he sneered at them,"that he made me his Vizier, a weak, witless fool who failed to purge vermin like you. This fire is no less than I deserve."

Even as the flames engulfed him, his final breaths echoed with shouts of your name.

To this day, men still say "loyal as Nawfal" when they speak of true service.

When you took power, Nawfal vanished from the capital.

And when you were overthrown and assassinated, he did not raise his voice in your defense. People whispered that he must have hated you still, that he reveled in your fall. But in secret, he rescued all those who had benefited from you and survived from new Sultan’s purge. In his hermitage, he established a school for the poorest children where the survivors became teachers. Years later, usurper's name faded into obscurity.

But the tales of you, [player.name], and that brief dawn when the reform sweeped the empire, spread across the land through the lips of the graduates.

To lend some semblance of stability to Sadani's son's reign, you named Nawfal your Vizier. Nawfal accepted it in silence.

He knew, just as you knew, the title demanded he bare his teeth against the realm's circling jackals, ever watchful for daggers in the dark, for poisoned whispers, for the slow erosion of his name. He even declined your rewards to uphold his political principles: "A crown's grace should not reward those already gorged on power."

For a fleeting time, the two of you almost believed change was possible. His pale hands steadied the scepter you could barely lift.

But two months later, Nawfal was assassinated.

The killers made little effort to hide their triumph. They celebrated death of the "Gadfly", that incorruptible, honestest man. With him gone, your rule bled from its first wound.

In those fleeting moments, you and Nawfal allowed yourselves... hope.

"Enough! The realm runs on the kind of men you just slaughtered!"

Then, ever the politician, she soothed them with gold and promises. The matter faded.

You still light candles for Nawfal each year. And by coincidence, the royal guard patrolled near that lonely grave, ensuring no vengeful hands disturb his rest.

Nawfal raged against your rule with such fervor that you finally snapped: "Save your breath, unless you mean to challenge me steel in hand."

On the day they killed you, he came to the fighting pit he'd never deigned to enter before. He gathered your broken body himself. Chose your resting place.

On the stone he set over your bones, beneath your name and dates, run a line carved small but deep:

"Had I been stronger, you might have been a good ruler."

Nawfal raged against your rule with such fervor that you finally snapped: "Save your breath, unless you mean to challenge me steel in hand."

When Sirshana fell and the crown passed to you, that pale adversary returned to court. He stood before your throne, staring through you with those unblinking eyes, then turned and walked away without a word.

You hadn't the courage to call him back.

Nawfal divided his days like a miser counting coins, the greater share for the realm's affairs, the lesser but brighter portion for tending the Nursery you'd establish together.

"You should rest," you often chided. He'd only smile and shake his head. "This is the sweetest dream I dare imagine. Why would I close my eyes and miss a moment of it?"

Years later, from that humble soil, generations of those seedlings would grow, until their intertwined hands raised the realm's first true university.

Nawfal died shortly after you.

The two of you remained hanging on the scaffolds, where passersby amused themselves by prodding your corpses with spears.

Before your bodies could fully rot, the great nobles seized control of the leaderless, chaotic realm. They swiftly reinstated every oppressive decree, going even further than the Sultan you had overthrown. Now every slave had to pay a monthly tax for the right to live, lest their masters slaughter them without consequence.

The nobles cheered this cruelty. They crushed the newly freed slaves with brutal fervor, and the slaves fought back with equal fury. The realm descended into a bloody stalemate. Occasionally, people still spoke of you... their voices thick with regret.

Your revolution had ended. But it planted seeds which would bloom, whether in ten years or a hundred.

Nawfal hung beside you on that cursed scaffold, and like you, was cut down before death could take him.

When consciousness returned, he bid you farewell without ceremony and rode home. There he shielded the Nursery you'd established together, hiring your loyalists as teachers, gathering kindred souls as students.

You never met again. Yet every few years, some bright-eyed youth would arrive at your cabin clutching a letter in Nawfal's precise hand.

You welcomed each with equal fervor, pouring your hard-won wisdom into their eager minds without complaint.

As for how those very youths would later raise your banner amidst the tides of chaos and forge a new realm in your image... well, that is a tale for another time.

Nawfal hung beside you on the scaffold.

Yet the moment the mob stormed in, the Vizier seemed to have lost all will to live. When your rescuers cut the ropes, they found him already gone.

They buried Nawfal near your woodland hut. No marker was placed, but a lone ironwood stood vigil over the grave. It straight as a spear, silent as the grave it guarded.

Nawfal was your staunchest ally. Without him, you might have abandoned your reforms long ago.

He stood with you against grasping lords and greedy nobles, yet also soothed the discontented smallfolk, those who'd hoped you'd be their perfect ruler, showering gold and pretty men and women upon them like spring rain.

Each night left you both exhausted beyond words, your eyes too weary to roll. Yet slowly, ever so slowly, you felt the great wheel of the realm creaking toward change. This fragile hope worked an unexpected change in Nawfal: he began training with the royal guards at dawn.

"Just... strengthening my body," he'd say between ragged breaths, "I mean to live long enough to see our work bear fruit. I'll not die before that day comes."

Nawfal remained a pillar of your court, tasked with uncovering the nobles' hidden truths. You bestowed upon him your own dagger with this decree: "Let this steel pierce any heart that dares hinder my will. All who oppose you are traitors by the crown's own word."

He took the dagger and vanished into the empire's shadowed corners, a ghost auditing your realm. Thrice each month bore his reports. The latest scroll read thus:

"To my sun bright Sultan - Your steel remains unbloodied, though my palm now wears the mark of its weight. To forge a realm where watchers need not draw blades... this is a labor worthy of your miracles. Each dawn I pray to see your dream endure another day. Each dusk I stand ready to die for it.

Now, as your foremost political adversary, I must critique your recent edicts. Do recall, no flattery lives in my ink.

[Continued for 46,425 words...]"

The chaos in the palace ended with the confirmation of your death. The rioters had never truly sought your life, and now stood dumbstruck, realizing too late that you alone had listened to their voices, that they'd just destroyed the first Sultan they'd ever raised up themselves.

Seizing the moment, Nawfal stepped forward, his pale face burning with fury as he denounced the mob for slaughtering the realm's last hope. With swift precision, he divided the crowd, commanding half to arrest the other. They obeyed without thinking, this pale noble's authority was absolute. The royal guards reformed their ranks. The man who'd toppled the throne with a tree was dragged away; the leaders who'd stormed the palace were pinned to the floor. Order returned like a tide washing blood from the steps. In the aftermath, the people's rage had burned itself out that night. Long they stood silent, as though unable to believe what hands had done.

For four years, Nawfal ruled as Sultan, but your crown and bloodstained robes remained upon the throne, and he would only stand beside it. He enforced your laws without mercy, reshaping the realm while summoning capable local officials to observe court. When the fourth winter came, he assembled a small council of seasoned, steel-true statesmen... then simply walked away. None in the capital ever saw his pale shadow again.

It was like some cruel dream, and that day never felt real. The terrible wound at your side ached when the rains came, and Nawfal would watch you with eyes full of grief and guilt.

Nawfal crushed the rebellion with ruthless efficiency. Together with Maggie, he made a spectacle of justice, and messengers stood in every marketplace in nobles’ lands, bellowing the gruesome details of how the rioters had been gelded as eunuchs.

As for the scheming nobles who'd stirred the pot? When you reclaimed the Golden Throne, they'd... vanished. "They were overcome with shame," Nawfal had claimed, "and willingly surrendered their lands." At least, that was what he'd said.

Nawfal was your most loyal comrade in the royal court. The ferocity he once directed against you was now unleashed on the Nobles challenging you. Gradually, you felt that this heavy cart was ever so slightly beginning to turn, and an unexpected change occurred in Nawfal: he began learning swordsmanship from the Court guards.

"I just want to make my Body stronger... healthier, so I can live longer," he told you, "I can't bear to die before seeing our reforms succeed."

Nawfal held nothing but contempt for Riel's brutish methods. Their heated quarrels echoed through the court with alarming regularity. Nawfal was, without question, among the realm's most brilliant, loyal, and capable minds - while Riel stood as the single most unreasonable, bullheaded, and utterly inflexible soul in all the empire. Watching them spar was endlessly entertaining, particularly knowing both fought solely for your benefit, without an ounce of self-interest between them... And each time, Nawfal's objections would soften just enough, while Riel's actions grew slightly more measured.

Ahem. Stop gawking and intervene - Riel's reaching for her sword!

Away from the court, Nawfal poured all his effort into the Nursery you'd established together. He expanded the school's walls, pried gold from tight-fisted nobles for its coffers. Two hundred children studied within, highborn and low, boys and girls, locals or outlanders alike. Only merit opened doors here; squandered chances meant no second ones.

Under Nawfal's careful tending, this Nursery grew silently through countless nights, and became the first true university this continent had ever known.

When the entire nation was left leaderless, Nawfal stood up and announced he would temporarily preside over the government, which left many Noblemen dissatisfied, wanting to seize the country while you were absent.

After clarifying the whole matter, Nawfal wrote a concise, elegant, and powerful article, inscribed on a Stone tablet, placed in the most conspicuous location before the palace. Passersby asked literate people to read those words; they included guarantees of why you overthrow the previous Sultan, and attempted to transform the country, and the Stone that struck you...

At the bottom of the inscription, Nawfal signed his name, along with a most vile Curse: "Anyone trying to cover up or erase this piece of history, will encounter Stones thrown at you, and by then, no Political Enemy will erect a monument for you."

This Stone stood behind you for many years, and no monarch or leader dared to shake it.

Nawfal had numerous opinions about your governance, so many that he argued with you daily, more than when serving as a Political Enemy or during the previous Sultan's games! Still, he argued more with Riel, since the Vizier hardly ever did what the Vizier was supposed to - it all depended on Nawfal's help!

Yet, he smiled more, and his brow eased; even when Riel angrily called him a molting Wild Dog, he could burst into laughter!

While you rode forth to quell rebellions, Nawfal remained in the Lapis Lazuli Palace, ruling in your stead. This silent understanding between you needed no words.

The sharp edge of his reproach had dulled with time. Now praise fell from his lips as often as counsel, though his gaze still held that old pity... tempered with hard-won respect.

Through this uneasy alliance, the Lapis Lazuli Palace saw your shadow linger longer. And you found more nights bearing the fleeting gift of sleep.

Nawfal barged into the royal palace immediately after your assassination attempt, locking down all gates of the capital to prevent the culprit's escape. Then, he, along with Alim, thoroughly investigated every Noble family; regardless of status or age, everyone was interrogated personally by him.

It is said that during the interrogations, he repeatedly scolded those Nobles, calling them ungrateful, shameless, shortsighted, and foolish; saying that they squandered the opportunity to improve this country.

After his tirades, he would silently slump down for a while, his face as white as a sheet.

After helping you purge all the noble houses involved in the rebellion, Nawfal closed the execution ledger with a weary hand and sighed.

"You nearly died," he said. "A hundred men surely died for this treason. Seven innocents burned in their homes. So much blood spilled just to kill a Sultan who sought to change this realm." He shook his head heavily. "I pity them."

Then he turned away to oversee the rebuilding of the fire-scarred streets.

Nawfal died shortly after you.

The two of you remained hanging on the scaffolds, where passersby amused themselves by prodding your corpses with spears.

Before your bodies could fully rot, the great nobles seized control of the leaderless, chaotic realm. They swiftly reinstated every oppressive decree, going even further than the Sultan you had overthrown. The nobles cheered this cruelty. They crushed the newly freed slaves with brutal fervor, and the slaves fought back with equal fury. The realm descended into a bloody stalemate. Occasionally, people still spoke of your brief reign with Nawfal... their voices thick with regret.

Your revolution had ended. But it planted seeds which would bloom, whether in ten years or a hundred.

You welcomed each with equal fervor, pouring your hard-won wisdom into their eager minds without complaint.

As for how those very youths would later raise your banner amidst the tides of chaos and forge a new realm in your image... well, that is a tale for another time.

They buried Nawfal near your woodland hut. No marker was placed, but a lone ironwood stood vigil over the grave. It straight as a spear, silent as the grave it guarded.

You were Nawfal's most loyal comrade, and he often said, "Without [player.name]'s support, I would have given up."

You not only helped him confront the greedy Nobles and lords, but also eased the Resentment of the people, who expected Nawfal to completely side with the monarch and were hoping to be showered with Gold Coins and gifted with handsome men and beautiful women from the palace!

Although at the end of each day, you two were so exhausted that you could scarcely move your eyes, gradually, you both indeed felt that this heavy carriage was ever so slightly beginning to turn. This filled you with hope and brought about an unexpected change in Nawfal: he began learning swordsmanship from the Court guards.

"I just want to make my Body stronger... healthier, so I can live longer," he told you, "I can't bear to die before seeing our reforms succeed."

As your Vizier, Nawfal despised nothing more than ease. He could never shake the conviction that reforming an empire so ancient should have required blood and toil. How could it have been this simple? All you did was slay one Dragon, a supernatural, transcendent, dimension-breaking beast of unmatched power, and suddenly the entire realm knelt at your feet?

Now, in addition to governing your court with meticulous fairness, your former political ‌adversary did something unprecedented: he hired swordsmen to train him in combat.

"If... if violence truly works... this well..." he panted between drills, sweat dripping from his brow, "...then I'll... try it too..."

Every time you made camp, a thick bundle of letters would arrive - all from Nawfal.

You didn't need to open them to know what they contained: The burdens of a Sultan, the state of the realm, the diplomatic fires sparked by conquest, the floods and famines, the cries of the people and reforms grinding to a halt.

All the things you had fought so hard to escape.

Nawfal lectured you, or we can say berated you, nearly every day.

It happened in court, at supper, in the royal library or along the vaulted corridors of the palace.

A hundred times you considered having him killed. Yet something stayed your hand. Some unnameable thing that would surely shatter if the deed were done.

You never knew precisely what it was. And still, to this day, he wearily, doggedly, went on lecturing.

epilogue_2000346.title: Epilogue: Jawad
strings: Jawad had followed you to this foreign land, abandoning his fortune, only to find his guts twisted with regret. Yet the man had a gift. He learned the tongue quickly enough, and soon discovered that one art transcended borders: the art of bribery. Before long, he left you behind, weaving himself into the schemes of borderland warlords. Through smuggling and monopoly, he amassed a fortune that would make even the Sultan's treasurers blush...

epilogue_2000350.title: Epilogue: Fardak
strings: Fardak remembered the path he paved with you at great risk. Later, he secretly returned alone along that route to his homeland, bringing back advanced technology and precious seeds. Yet, he no longer seemed to adapt to homeland life – he spent his lifetime traversing that trade route...

epilogue_2000352.title: Epilogue: Mahir
strings: Mahir arrived with you in this strange eastern land, where the very air hummed with unfamiliar knowledge. She drank it all in, thirsty as a desert wanderer at an oasis. In time, she built for the emperor the tallest tower and grandest statue the world had ever seen, and made them could shift form and emit destructive beams. These magnificent creations were only activated at thirty percent capacity during a failed palace coup. The High Constables destroyed them before you could witness their full horror. Nevertheless, they obliterated several years' worth of the imperial budget, as undisputed weapons of terror.

epilogue_2000369.title: Epilogue: Aziz
strings: Aziz lumbered into his new appointed role with deliberate slowness. From somewhere unknown, he conjured a band of hardened followers who stood firmly behind him. Within a few short years, the hulking former slave had risen to become a high noble whose voice carried weight in the new regime.

Aziz was named one of your iron guards, and he accepted the honor in silence.

Afterward, he formed a guard of his own where men as silent and towering as he, sons of the steppes. They brought their families with them, and now the capital teemed with tall, dusk-skinned folk. Stern-faced they stood, yet their eyes burned with unconcealed wonder and eagerness, hungry to know this new world.

When the empire's unrest had nearly settled, Aziz came before you. He knelt and begged leave to seek out his people.

"We are no weaker than the wild tribes," he said. "We can serve the Sultan. We will not be slaves, but we can be his subjects. I will make them see reason."

You granted his request. And since he had been raised to nobility and given a post at court, it was only fitting he hold lands of his own. With so many dead nobles of late... it was no trouble to carve out fertile pastures for him.

He bowed in gratitude and departed. Three months passed before he returned with thousands of tall, silent steppe-folk at his back.

They settled within the empire, the first of their kind to swear fealty to the Sultan. How Aziz had swayed those proud, hardened people, you did not know. Nor did you ask.

epilogue_2000370.title: Epilogue: Zephyr
strings: Zephyr found the steppes near the hermitage most pleasing. Between duties, he would often race across the plains, returning with armfuls of wildflowers clutched to his chest. He remained cheerful as ever, yet beneath his laughter lay sorrows so deep that only when he ran himself to exhaustion could he briefly escape them.

He would first present the flowers to the lady of the house, then leave a portion in your study. The brightest blooms he saved - these he would tuck with tender care into his wife's thick, dark tresses.

The gilded halls of the court made Zephyr itch with unease, his toes curled restlessly against the cold lapis lazuli floors. Yet let any courtier dare breathe a word against you, and the former slave would spring to his feet like a hound unleashed. When words failed him, he'd challenge the offender to a racing duel! As none ever accepted these peculiar invitations, Zephyr maintained an unbroken record of victories.

epilogue_2000371.title: Epilogue: Inal
strings: Inal's cooking grew ever more masterful, and Maggie granted her a generous daily purse to scour the local markets for the finest seasonal fare. Her roasted quail and braised rabbit proved so exquisite... Since retreating from court life, both you and Maggie had begun developing rather unfortunate waistlines.

Aziz lumbered into his new appointed role with deliberate slowness. From somewhere unknown, he conjured a band of hardened followers who stood firmly behind him. Within a few short years, the hulking former slave had risen to become a high noble whose voice carried weight in the new regime. His wife managed the sprawling new household, dispatching messengers repeatedly to your hermitage to bombard Maggie with endless "What should we do about this?" and "How should we handle that?". On numerous occasions, people overheard this newly ascended noble couple speaking of you with reverent conviction. "My Master - oh, even now that I'm no longer a slave, I'll still call him that! - is the finest man alive, don't you agree, dear?" "Yes."

After parting from her mistress, Inal's cheer long faded. Truth be told, you avoided her, for her face was too much a reminder of Maggie. The way Maggie would scold her for chattering too much, the way she'd laugh and press coins into her palm for quail at the market, the way she'd guide her hands in mending a seam... Not long after your retreat to this place, Inal came before you with a small pouch of coins, her own meager savings. And then, she placed in your hands a slip of parchment. "Let her buy her freedom at a fair price," Maggie had written. You granted the girl her liberty. She knelt one last time, forehead pressed to the floor, then rose and left. More than once, you nearly called her back to demand why Maggie had left words for her alone. And what of you? No final counsel? But... no. You were tired. let it be then.

Aziz and Inal became your most trusted hands at court. You gave Aziz free rein to forge a guard loyal to you alone: men and women of any birth, any blood, their only creed being fealty. As for Inal, she seized the mantle of chief handmaiden with fierce determination. "Those clumsy noble girls can't even fold a bedsheet properly!" she scoffed. 

Now, the couple stood as pillars of your rule. When you held council, Aziz loomed at your side like a great, silent sentinel, flanked by his equally grim and towering sworn guards. Meanwhile, his wife glided through the halls, bearing cups of tart pomegranate juice, cool and crimson. "Brewed to the Sultan's queen's own taste," she declared proudly to all who would listen. "Her favorite since she was a little girl!"

You gave Aziz free rein to forge a guard loyal to you alone, but the old nobles shackled his efforts at every turn. When the time came, he had barely mustered five men. Inal, whom you named Chamberlain of the court, was treated like a plague by the highborn. The noble ladies never fully bent to her command. 

On the night you fell, it was Inal who took the first arrow meant for you, her frail body shielding yours. Aziz and his brothers cut down forty-seven assassins before the forty-eighth blade found them. As they lay dying, their gaze held yours, calm and unwavering. Had their lungs still drawn breath, had their throats still formed words, they would have whispered: "In the next life... we would still stand at your side."

You tasked Aziz with forging a personal guard, answering to none but you. "No highborn pups," you warned. Months later, the silent giant returned and knelt with twelve horselords as towering as himself. From that hour, your life rested in their calloused hands. 

Inal became responsible for supplying this guard. You'd never trust those simpering eunuchs or noble girls with such work. Once, you nearly assigned guards to protect Inal, before realizing the folly: Where would it end? 

Yet they served flawlessly. In their steadfast presence, the ever-present tension in your shoulders would ease, sometimes. Yet once a year, Inal would test your patience. She insisted on lighting candles in a secluded rose garden, murmuring prayers for "her dearest mistress." This year, you resisted the urge to have her head struck off. Next year? Well, who knows?
Inal would never leave Maggie, remaining ever her mistress's devoted servant. The lively children she bore with Aziz brought rare laughter to the melancholy Maggie.

epilogue_2000372.title: Epilogue: Faraj
strings: Faraj followed you, served you, devoted his life to you. It is through his pen that history knows your words and deeds— –refined, distilled, polished into philosophical scripture. He discarded the frivolous, sculpted the noble, and forged a school of thought in your name. Centuries later, scholars from your homeland rediscovered his writings. Through them, your ideas became a bridge between the old faith and the new land. As your name rose in prominence, some even revered you as a prophet.

The long journey tempered Faraj into something greater – a man of equal parts wisdom and courage. A decade passed in the East before he heard of his homeland’s fate: his ancestral lands, gnawed by feckless heirs. He gathered allies from every road you had walked together, and crossed the continent once more, to bring justice to his birthright. So another great epic was born.

As long as you remained, Faraj would love this family you had made and all its members. In time, he even convinced other brilliant men and women to join it. He was a steward, a teacher, a guardian. Without his encouragement, the household would not have grown so vast, nor the children so many... though it was always hard to know who the father was exactly. But the world was wide enough for you to find a haven, and your hearts were expansive enough to cradle such joy.

You left Faraj in the political center. The night before you left for your retreat, he asked you countless questions, writing them down as he did; by sunrise, the rolls of parchment he held were more than half a person high. Later, people often said, 'Faraj seems like another [player.name],' with political views, behavior, likes and dislikes, even his attire increasingly resembling yours. Perhaps this is his way of missing you.

Faraj became your servant, the steward of your days. His ledger grew thick with your every word and deed, even the idle "This tea scalds" was inscribed, as though each syllable were sacred.

Being the servant of Sultan had always been greased with gold. At first, the nobles came as they had under the old Sultan, pouches heavy with coin, seeking favor. Faraj drove them out like stray dogs, considering it as great insult. Thus did history record him: the first servant who refused even a single copper in the empire’s history.

Faraj rode back to his own lands, though you had urged him to stay... "A duty weighs upon me," he said. "I will tell every soul the tale of how you crushed the tyrant and saved the realm. Many still do not know this truth, so I shall begin in my own lands, and make certain no man forgets your legend!" And so he set forth, with unwavering confidence.

Faraj was among your most ardent supporters, zealously implementing your reforms in his lands.

When word of the palace atrocities finally reached his remote domain seven days late, he rallied every soul who could wield a blade and marched on the capital that very night.

By the time he stormed the city, you had just regained consciousness, weak but alive, and received him in your sickbed. At the sight of your gaunt, bandaged form, Faraj erupted in fury. "Those wretches never deserved such a great Sultan!" he roared, ready to personally behead the prisoners until you seized his arm and pleaded. What you needed most, you told him, was not vengeance, but a true friend to carry on the reforms.

Faraj wept at your bedside, then obeyed.

His people, who had witnessed it all, spread the tale far and wide with embellishment, of course. "Our lord is the Sultan's closest friend," they declared, and the claim proved invaluable in rallying support. Years later, Faraj's lands flourished under his governance, transformed into a jewel of the empire.

After your coronation, Faraj devoted himself chiefly to writing.

He was then composing “The Grand Chronicles of [player.name] - Volume III”. This seven-volume chronicle was meant to record every detail of your existence, including how you had wailed at birth (having tracked down your old wet nurse, he had interrogated her for three days), what you had favored as a child, even the last time you had wet your bed... It was said three more years would yet be needed before he could set down the moment you had slain the dragon.

Faraj now served as your messenger, tasked with gathering knowledge and seeking the next prey.

Whispers spoke of a colossal ice golem slumbering atop the mountain peaks, of a magma worm in the fiery depths of the volcano, larger than the royal palace itself... These were queer tales and half-heard rumors Faraj collected and laid before you.

strings: Of course, Lady Becky had remained with you, He would tolerate no other humans but you and Maggie. Now she prowled Maggie’s garden, a sleek shadow amidst the blossoms, batting at butterflies and toying with crickets. That was far better sport than any gilded palace!

About Lady Becky, well, why on earth would you keep a little kitten at court? Now no one tread the lapis lazuli floors care for politics. They only wonder: Whom will Lady Beige favor today? Who shall be blessed as his scratching post?

Lady Becky never cared for your embrace, yet with Maggie gone, he endured your company as a lesser choice. Reluctantly, she relocated with you to the hermitage, hunting insects in your overgrown garden. Sometimes, she would curl up on Maggie clothes for a nap.

Lady Becky hold the esteemed title of Chief Mouser to the Court, though naturally, he finds the actual work beneath her. Why trouble his royal paws with hunting when the chefs serve delicacies on velvet cushions?

Why trouble her royal paws with hunting when the chefs serve delicacies on velvet cushions? And no, he did’t care that you were politically strangled and discomforts. He’s a cat. What did you expect?

When you were assassinated, Lady Becky's snowy fur was streaked with blood. As the handmaidens pried him from your lifeless body, he thrashed and keened like a mourner at a pyre.

From that day forth, white cats bearing splash-red markings were bred throughout the realm. The blood-marked breed came to be called "Lady Becky," and so it endures.

And no, he did’t care that you were politically strangled and discomforts. He’s a cat. What did you expect?

Lady Becky cared not for your Realm of Game. So long as you fed him shredded chicken with your own hands, anointed him with plaice pâté, and scratched the base of him tail, you were deemed a most worthy servant in the eyes of this little kitty.

Lady Becky hold the esteemed title of Chief Mouser to the Court, though his chief duty lies in... assessing the winds of favor.

Should Zazie enter the palace first, the cat would settle upon her lap with practiced devotion. Yet if you strode in before Zazie, Lady Becky would scale your robes without hesitation.

Thus did you and Zazie arrive at court ever earlier, until you summoned Mr.Longman, a tom to claim Zazie’s affections.

The palace was thick with prowling kittens, and no matter the hour, you'd always find one curled up on your knee.

You had the outer garden of the palace cleared to house the new government, and soon the court swelled with comings and goings.

The most immediate consequence was this: Lady Becky grew fat, for nearly every soul who laid eyes upon his returned a second time with chicken strips or dried fish hidden in their sleeves.

Thus were two ironclad laws set in your court: First, that none should hinder the great empire’s march forward; and second, that none should feed the cat.

When the tale turned amusing, a maiden's laughter drifted down from beyond the twelfth heaven... "Thank you for bringing me books," she whispered. "You are the kindest master."

In the heart of the royal court, you raised a humble altar to a forgotten Star-Souled - Lumera. Each day, you had your lettered handmaidens read passages before it, fearing the void between stars might hold no books to ease her solitude.

epilogue_2000771.title: Epilogue: Riel
strings:
You would rule not just the court, but also the shadowed alleys, the narrow lanes, the slums, all territories of Riel. She could slip through them like an loach or strike your enemies like a scorpion lurking in the mud. 

You told Riel that henceforth, she would be your hand and your eyes. Her gang would no longer be outlaws, but the Sultan's Security team. They could lawfully collect their dues, though far less than before, and you would make up the difference. 

Riel didn't fully grasp your words, but her gang did. The rogues, the cutthroats, the scoundrels, they all dropped to their knees before you in unison. This was something they could never have achieved on their own: They could now serve the Sultan. 

"Well..." Riel said slowly, kneeling as well, the first time you had ever seen her bend the knee, even if only one touched the ground. "If this pleases the rest... then I'll take it. I'll serve you. Not like what I do will change much, right?" 

And it didn't. For years to come, she and her gang, well, let's say Security team, kept the capital in order.

Your dominion extends beyond the court to the alleys, small streets, and slums. These places are Riel's territory, where she can dart around like an eel and sting your enemies fiercely like a scorpion in the mud. 

Riel became your representative on the dark side of the city. In over seventy days of your reign, you cooperated seamlessly. When the news of your assassination came, Riel rushed to the streets with her people—only to realize there was nothing she could do. 

Changing the country would not be the work of brute force, and consuming a hundred livers would not bring back a Sultan. 

She retreated into the alleys, committed to collaborating with everyone opposing the new ruler. She took over your guesthouse, making it the opposition's headquarters. "When he was alive, I was quite foolish," Riel once spoke of you. "It was not until he died that I realized what he taught me. That guy was a good man."

For years to come, she and her gang, well, let's say Security team, kept the capital in order. Often you wondered: had Riel not ruled the city's scum and wretches with her fists and teeth... might you have been lying dead in some gutter long ago?

You would rule not just the court, but also the shadowed alleys, the narrow lanes, the slums, all territories of Riel. She could slip through them like an loach or strike your enemies like a scorpion lurking in the mud.

Riel became your voice in the city's underbelly. For the seventy-odd days of your reign, the two of you worked seamlessly together. But when news of your assassination reached her, she stormed the streets with her gang, only to realize there was nothing she could do. It could not be changed by brutes. No amount of devoured livers could bring a Sultan back to life.

So she retreated into the shadows and made common cause with every enemy of the new Sultan. She took over your Guesthouse, turning them into a stronghold for dissent.

When news of your assassination reached Riel, she stormed the streets with her gang, only to realize there was nothing she could do. It could not be changed by brutes. No amount of devoured livers could bring a Regent back to life.

So she retreated into the shadows and made common cause with every enemy of Zazie. She took over your Guesthouse, turning them into a stronghold for dissent.

Years later, the slum-dwellers whispered that the city had two female Sultan: one a spider spinning golden webs, the other a wolf who fed on livers.

Riel was the last king of the Realm of Jungle you had built.

She had slain her rivals, devoured their livers, until none dared challenge her.

The once-glorious royal cloak now hung in tatters, the kingdom crumbling to dust. So Riel gathered those still willing to follow, and turned her back on the cold iron throne. She would carve out new lands with her own hands.

Her host grew with each passing league: starving peasants, abused slaves, tribes driven from their homelands. They marched behind their king with crude weapons and solemn eyes, a ragged tide of the desperate.

Ancient kingdoms shattered before them. Like some great river catfish, Riel's horde churned the waters wherever they passed, scattering the old order like frightened minnows.

Thus the continent was plunged into endless war. But from those dark jungles, new kingdoms would rise with new laws and hope.

Riel was granted command of the capital's watch by King Sirshana's decree. That was your advice, though soon the king himself grew fonder of her than you'd ever been. Their tastes aligned perfectly: the same faces bruised under their fists, the same stinking taverns known by heart, the same glee in a good tavern brawl. With the new king's blessing, Riel seized control of the city's peacekeeping—her method simple as it was brutal: beat them until they stopped moving.

Then came Sirshana's fall. Old enemies crawled from every shadow. Riel slept with blades in hand, if she slept at all. You offered sanctuary within the palace walls, but she refused.

"Hide beneath your wings again, and the city will say Riel's just a king's lapdog. Then I'm done."

So she chose a different refuge: the fighting pits. Day after day, she entered the bloody sands. One by one, her foes fell before her in single combat. After each victory, she'd paint her face with their blood, raising crimson hands to the roaring crowd as she circled the arena.

You put Riel in charge of the city's underbelly, especially after the slaves were freed. Vagrants flooded the capital, bringing chaos in their wake.

Riel didn't fully understand your reforms, but she stood with you instinctively. Freedom couldn't be bad, could it? So she took up her dagger, gathered her thugs, and donned the blood-red uniforms you provided, then began patrolling the streets.

Her methods were simple: beat them. But now that she served the Sultan, she held back somewhat. Before, she left men ten-tenths dead; now, five or seven would suffice. The city grew quieter under her fist, and her ranks swelled with freed slaves who were strong, hardened men.

Then came the runaways. They'd heard of the Sultan's decree, but their masters refused to obey. So they fled, with slavers hot on their heels. Riel took them in. She broke the bones of famous slave-catchers, then begged you for the worst jobs like hauling water, carting shit, tanning hides, anything to put the fugitives to work. Each week, she paid them a pittance, a few coppers. That were their first wages, their first property.

"All thanks to the Sultan," she'd growl at them, "so if you disobey me, which means disobeying the Sultan, 'cause he's my damn brother! And I'll eat your livers raw!"

Ha! No one in the court dared praise the beauty of Riel's eyes anymore.

The good news was that Vizier, she had finally learned to bathe and comb her hair. The bad news? Her taste for human livers had never waned. Through all those years serving you, Riel had cheerfully devoured countless steaming livers—so many, in fact, that she had grown somewhat plump from them.

Riel roared as she tore open the belly of the first stone-thrower, ripping out his liver with her bare hands. Only then did the mob realize what they'd done—they had killed the Sultan.

For a fleeting moment, the rioters wavered. Hands clutching stones began to tremble. The fire of rage cooled, replaced by cold dread as consequences took shape in their minds. They exchanged fearful glances, blaming the men beside them who urged this... certainly not their doing.

But Riel cared nothing for such thoughts. Where she saw guilt, she delivered death.。

That day, in retribution, Riel and her gang slaughtered six hundred and forty rioters in the streets. Following the traditions of her homeland against slavers, she impaled every corpse upon the trees. When the work was done, she gathered her followers and abandoned the kingdom. She was never meant to be a protector of good men, and better to return to the mud, to simpler lands where justice needed no pretense.

The stench of death lingered over the capital for months.

Riel traveled at your side across the length and breadth of the realm, and as your shield against danger, your most vocal critic on every decree. The wildling woman grew ever broader, ever taller, exulting in each new sight the world revealed. Her understanding of the empire deepened with each passing day. Watching her was like witnessing a sapling surge skyward with unnatural speed. At times, you allowed yourself a flicker of warmth: might this woman one day bear the weight of the empire upon her shoulders?

It was a foolish hope. But even fools may kindle embers of defiance against fate.

Riel avenged you in her own fashion. She hunted down every last coin-greased hand—the killers who struck for gold, the arsonists who lit their torches for silver, even the wretches who'd prepared damp cloths for the murderers. She slaughtered them all.

But she refused to eat their livers, deeming them filthy.

You had Riel dispose of many corpses for you. At first, she reveled in it—good coin, fresh livers to eat, and the satisfaction of serving you.

But even she, in time, came to you with grave words.

"Kill too many," she said, meeting your gaze without flinching, "and sooner or later, you'll start wanting to kill yourself too. The mightiest warriors of my people all died that way."

You turned your face away and did not look at her again.

Zephyr and Arumina stood at the heart of your rescue: had he not outrun the hunters, they would have caught you before the city gates; without Arumina's gold, they could never have drowned every cutthroat in wine...

Those bright kids had Arumina's pride and Zephyr's quickness in their bones.

strings:
The conference opened with Professor Huanita presenting a paper titled "On the Desultanization Process Led by [player.name]."
